paragraphs: CleanSpark, a bitcoin miner moving into AI data centers, is building two large sites in Texas over local opposition. In Austin County, near Sealy, it plans a 285-megawatt data center on about 270 acres; in Brazoria County, south of Houston, a site that would start at 300 megawatts and could grow to 600. Both are proposed, with construction not yet begun. In Georgia, CleanSpark already operates a growing 175-megawatt data center in Sandersville under a 20-year lease with an unnamed tenant.

On August 14, 2026, dozens of Austin County residents drove tractors and trucks to a CleanSpark community meeting near Trenckmann Road and FM 949 to protest the Sealy site, citing water, noise, light and wildlife concerns. "We are not going to lay down and take it. We are here to fight," resident Lisa Hicks said. CleanSpark said it would build its own substation, pay for grid upgrades, and use closed-loop cooling. On July 27, 2026, Austin County commissioners voted unanimously for a moratorium on data centers and battery storage systems, covering all such projects, not just CleanSpark's.

In Brazoria County, commissioners voted unanimously in June 2026 for a resolution opposing any future data center that does not protect grid reliability, water, farmland and public infrastructure; it is not a ban, and County Judge L.M. "Matt" Sebesta Jr. said it carries little real force without state action. Two days before the Sealy protest, Governor Greg Abbott said CleanSpark, Google and Rowan had agreed to comply with state data center standards requiring disclosure of power, water and incentive details to regulators.

CleanSpark has operated in Sandersville, Georgia, since 2022. Its July 2026 lease there covers 175 megawatts of IT capacity and could bring $6.6 billion in revenue over the term; the same tenant signed a letter of intent covering CleanSpark's 718-acre, 885-megawatt Texas portfolio. CleanSpark has described the tenant only as a "high investment-grade, leading global technology company" and has not named it in the sources used for this page.

EdgeConneX, a data center developer owned by the investment firm EQT, ran into organized opposition on two of its largest 2026 proposals. In Douglas County, Georgia, commissioners voted 4-1 in early July to deny a rezoning for a five-building, roughly 700-acre campus near Villa Rica, after the county planning commission had recommended denial. One resident told commissioners, "We already have 11 data centers. That's ridiculous!"

Commissioner Mark Alcarez, whose district includes the site, voted against the rezoning but noted the county's budget needs: "We are 25 years behind in our road infrastructure. That money has got to come from somewhere." Supporters had pointed to a projected 200 to 300 permanent jobs; it is not known whether the developer will return with a modified plan.

In the Village of Ashville, Ohio, EdgeConneX planned a 680-acre campus with a 1.8-gigawatt substation. After the village council adopted a term summary with the company in April 2026 that would have exempted the project from an existing moratorium, resident Laura McNamara-Smith and others petitioned for a referendum; the Ohio Supreme Court ordered it placed before the Pickaway County Board of Elections.

On August 24, 2026, the board voted unanimously to put the referendum on the November 3, 2026 ballot for village voters. The Circleville Herald noted the ballot question is on the council's resolution itself, not a direct vote for or against the data center.

EdgeCore is a Denver-based wholesale data center developer, launched in 2018 and bought by the private equity firm Partners Group in 2022, that builds campuses for single large tenants. In Culpeper, Virginia, it announced in July 2024 that it had bought 120 acres in the Culpeper Technology Zone for a 1.4 million-square-foot campus.

DatacenterDynamics reported the campus would start at 216 megawatts of IT load and could reach 432 megawatts, with first power from Rappahannock Electric Cooperative expected in early 2028; EdgeCore's own campus page now gives an initial phase of 196 megawatts in two buildings totaling 920,000 square feet. By April 2026, Virginia Business reported, construction had begun.

In Mesa, Arizona, DCD reported in May 2025 that EdgeCore was adding 43.87 acres to its existing 40-acre campus, raising capacity from more than 200 megawatts to more than 450 megawatts, with power from Salt River Project; the campus is operating and expanding. Its Santa Clara, California campus is operating at 72 megawatts, and a campus near Reno, Nevada, in McCarran, is under construction.

Global Stack is a Southern California company, registered in March 2026, that has been pitching California's state-run fairgrounds on 100-year land leases for what it calls emergency-resilience infrastructure: shipping-container-sized computing units, multi-story parking garages and "vertiports" for helicopters and passenger drones. DatacenterDynamics reported in July 2026 that the company intends to build such sites on at least 70 fairgrounds by 2030, with data center units of up to about 10 megawatts. Global Stack says it is not building traditional data centers and that its units use closed-loop cooling and little water. Residents at meeting after meeting have disputed that description. At the Ventura County Fairgrounds in September 2026, CEO Dan Kang said, "We're not a data center," but acknowledged the unit would be considered a data center "in general governance," the Ojai Valley News reported.

The strongest pushback has come in the San Joaquin Valley and on the coast. On July 21, 2026, 29 people spoke against the proposal for the Kings County Fairgrounds at a packed Hanford City Council meeting, and none spoke in favor, the Hanford Sentinel reported. Mayor Mark Kairis said the city had not been consulted, and City Attorney Ty Mizote noted the fairgrounds are owned by the state. "The general rule is state agencies are not subject to local laws," he said, adding that the city council may have no authority to prohibit the project. Resident Amy Briar said her electric bill had reached $1,200 a month. The same day in Tulare, a fair board tabled a Global Stack lease item after more than two hours of public comment, KMPH reported. On Sept. 15, 2026, the Ventura County Fair Board voted 5-3 to give Global Stack a 30-day notice ending a nonbinding memorandum of understanding for a 5-acre waterfront site, after a meeting attended by about 200 people. "This project is not right for the fairgrounds," board member Miriam Mack said. The Ventura City Council voted unanimously the same day to send a letter opposing the project.

Earlier, according to DCD, the Calistoga fairgrounds advisory committee discontinued talks with the company after public backlash, and the Solano County fair described the idea as "basically tabled." At the Cow Palace in Daly City, the arena's CEO said in July 2026 that it was still evaluating a proposal and had made no decision. In August 2026 the San Francisco Chronicle reported that Michael Flores, the state's deputy secretary for fairs and expositions, had made introductions and attended pitch meetings for Global Stack while his daughter worked for the company. A spokesperson for Gov. Gavin Newsom told the paper, "Our office is investigating these claims."
/company/global-stack/.unconfirmed: The Business Journal (Fresno) and YourCentralValley returned JS challenges/access denied. KMPH's story is datelined Tulare and describes the 24th District Agricultural Association board but also names the Kings County Fairgrounds, so the report says only that 'a fair board in Tulare' tabled the item. The site's 'Suspended' status for Hanford was not confirmed in any article read. Hoodline results were excluded.

paragraphs: Google is Belgium's biggest data center builder. It runs a campus at Saint-Ghislain in Hainaut province, open since 2010 and its first in Europe, and is building a second, three-building campus on 53 hectares of the Ecopôle business park at Farciennes, near Charleroi. A third Google site, at Feluy-Écaussinnes, has a permit but no high-voltage grid connection yet; Wallonia's economy minister, Pierre-Yves Jeholet, said the goal is for it to open in 2029.

The neighbors notice the growth. Anne More, 68, lives 200 meters from the Saint-Ghislain buildings and told the magazine Médor that a new extension under construction is causing trouble, noise first of all; she bought headphones to block it out. At Farciennes, which the Brussels Times called Wallonia's poorest municipality, about 100 delegates of the FGTB union protested at the construction site on March 24, 2026, and were refused permission to meet the foreign workers employed there.

Google said the Farciennes campus, part of a 1 billion euro investment, would bring about 100 permanent jobs; Saint-Ghislain employs more than 400 people. The permit requires rooftop solar, 95 percent carbon-free energy by 2030, air cooling in place of water-hungry systems, and a link to a district heating network. The grid operator Elia confirmed 200 to 300 megawatts of power for the site. Power is now the main limit: until Elia upgrades its lines, the local distributor Ores will connect the Feluy site only temporarily, at medium voltage.
Near Brussels, Digital Realty runs a data center on Mercuriusstraat in Zaventem.

Rio de Janeiro's biggest data center plan is Rio AI City, a campus at the former Olympic Park in the Southwest Zone that Elea Data Centers is developing with City Hall. On June 8, 2026, Elea announced a US$550 million investment and signed a 36-month cooperation agreement with Mayor Eduardo Cavaliere. It plans 1.5 gigawatts of power at first, rising to 3 gigawatts by 2032, with Elea's existing RJO1 data center already running on the project and new buildings to follow.

Where the power comes from is still an open question. When then-Mayor Eduardo Paes launched it in April 2025, promising clean energy and "unlimited" water, City Hall did not answer the energy outlet eixos about where the electricity would come from. A Federal University of Rio de Janeiro researcher, Piero Carlo Sclaverano dos Reis, has said the campus could need up to 3 gigawatts, more than the metro area's average load of about 1.8 gigawatts. Elea's architects promise certified renewable power and cooling that uses no water.

Rio already has several working data centers, most of them in the North Zone. Ascenty runs two in Pavuna, of 10 and 3 megawatts, in an area RioOnWatch says is known for water shortages and power outages. Equinix operates RJ1 in Botafogo and RJ2 in Del Castilho, and ODATA, owned by Aligned Data Centers, runs its RJ01 site. Asked for data on the energy and water use of the city's data centers, the municipal environment office told RioOnWatch the information did not exist in its systems.

Kymenlaakso, the southeastern Finnish region around Kouvola and Hamina, has Google's longest-running Finnish data center and two newer campuses under way. Google has operated in Hamina since 2009, when it converted an old paper mill on the coast into a data center, and has invested €4.5 billion there over 15 years, according to Helsinki Times. On Sept. 9, 2026, Google announced it would invest at least €13 billion in Finland over 2027 and 2028, expanding Hamina and building three new facilities in Kajaani, Vaala and Muhos, plans Yle reported had earlier been put on ice while the company waited on the government's proposed removal of a tax benefit. The company tied the expansion to a 22-year power purchase agreement with Fortum for up to half the output of the Loviisa nuclear plant.

In Kouvola, a developer called Hyperco is building a data center that TikTok says will become part of Project Clover, its €12 billion program aimed at strengthening protections for European user data. According to an economic assessment commissioned by TikTok and Hyperco and reported by CNBC in September 2026, construction of a 50-megawatt first phase began in September 2025 and is due to finish in 2027, with a second phase adding 100 megawatts. A TikTok spokesperson told CNBC it would become a tenant only once the facility was available for use.

Also in Kouvola, the Nordic operator atNorth is building its FIN04 campus in Ummeljoki/Myllykoski. The company first described a 23-hectare, 60-megawatt site in late 2023 and now lists it at up to 430 megawatts across 45 hectares, DCD reported in February 2026, when atNorth applied for a building permit for three more data center buildings and the local council was set to discuss the request. Yle reported the first building broke ground in 2024 and is due to go live in the first half of 2027. The site is to connect to the district heating network run by the local utility KSS Energia.

Data centers have not always been welcomed in Finland. At the September 2026 announcement Prime Minister Petteri Orpo acknowledged as much, saying that "In public debate in Finland, the impact of data centres on employment is often underestimated. I find this peculiar in a country that has struggled with high unemployment for a long time." Yle noted that critics focus on the draw on local resources and on climate impact. No council decision on atNorth's February 2026 permit request has been publicly reported.
/data-centers/finland/kymenlaakso/.unconfirmed: Dropped the separate €1 billion Hamina expansion (seventh expansion, 100 jobs) and the 1,400-hectare Metsähallitus land deal, which appeared only in search snippets. Dropped the YIT €300 million construction contract for FIN04 (not read). Did not find the outcome of the Kouvola council discussion of atNorth's permit. Did not find local Finnish-language coverage of objections in Kouvola or Hamina.

paragraphs: The main data center project in South Ostrobothnia is a campus being built by Pure DC, a British developer, in the Kivenneva area of Seinäjoki, the regional capital. According to Yle, the project was first discussed publicly in 2021. In late 2025 the city council was due to approve a zoning change that merged a block of just over 22 hectares along Itäväylä into a single plot. The building permit was handled in February 2026. It covers 21 buildings in total, three of them data center buildings, and the rest supporting structures. In April 2026 the city sold the 22.3-hectare plot to Pure DC Projects Oy for about 3.86 million euros, which Yle called the largest land sale in the city's history. The city and the company have preliminary agreements covering the sale of a 155-hectare area, so the site could grow. Earthworks had already started near the junction of Peräseinäjoentie and the eastern bypass.

In July 2026 Pure DC formally launched the first phase: 110 megawatts, costing about 1.5 billion euros, on a campus the company says could eventually exceed 550 megawatts and a total investment of more than 7.5 billion euros. Pure DC told Yle the first phase was already fully leased. Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that Microsoft is among the tenants, and DCD reported that neither company had confirmed it. Pure DC says the site has its permits, grid connection and a substation for the first building in place. It says the campus will use direct liquid cooling in closed loops with no water use in operation, according to Computer Weekly. The company says the first phase will bring about 1,500 construction jobs. An April 2026 Yle report put permanent jobs at 150.

The city's case rests on jobs, taxes and heat. "As well as the construction jobs and permanent roles there will be many other benefits for the area – business rates and property tax will be reinvested to benefit local residents, waste heat from the data center will be repurposed for our district heating network, and our partnership will also see Pure DC investing across a number of education and reskilling initiatives," Seinäjoki mayor Jaakko Kiiskilä said in the July announcement. No published report describes organized local opposition or any vote against the project. Seinäjoki is not the only place in the region courting data centers: Yle noted that the small municipality of Isojoki had approved a letter of intent for one.
/data-centers/finland/south-ostrobothnia.unconfirmed: The Yle zoning story (74-20199368) has no date in the extracted text. Its timing (late 2025, with the council vote on 15.12.2025) comes from the city's plan document URL in search results, which I did not read. The report therefore does not say whether the council actually approved the change. I did not read the Isojoki project story, so it is mentioned only as Yle's link headline states it. I could not verify Microsoft's tenancy beyond Bloomberg's unnamed sources as relayed by DCD and Computer Weekly. The Ilkka-Pohjalainen article was not read. The permanent-jobs figure (150) comes from Yle in April 2026, when the operator was not yet named.

paragraphs: County Galway's one well-known data center project, Apple's planned campus at Derrydonnell Woods outside Athenry, never got built. Apple announced the greenfield project in February 2015. Galway County Council granted permission that September, subject to conditions, and after an appeal and oral hearings An Bord Pleanála confirmed it in August 2017, RTÉ reported. The Irish Times reported that the €850 million project was expected to employ 150 technical staff once finished and would have been the largest single private-sector investment in Connacht. More than 2,000 people marched in Athenry in November 2016 to support it after objections put it on hold.

Objectors, including Sinead Fitzpatrick and Allan Daly, challenged the board's approval in the courts. According to The Irish Times, they argued that An Bord Pleanála should have assessed the environmental impact of Apple's full masterplan of eight data halls, which would have raised demand on the national grid by 6 to 8 per cent, and not only the first hall. On May 10, 2018, Apple said it would not go ahead, blaming "delays in the approval process." The minister for business, Heather Humphreys, said the delays had "underlined our need to make the State's planning and legal processes more efficient."

Apple then tried to sell the site. With the original permission due to run out in September 2021, the company applied for a five-year extension, and the council granted it in August 2021. Allan Daly and the group Eco-Advocacy challenged that decision in the High Court. In June 2022 the High Court quashed the extension, with the consent of lawyers for both the council and the State, RTÉ reported. The objectors had argued that the council did not assess the extension's implications as EU law requires and did not let the public make submissions. The earlier permission has expired, so anyone who wants to build a data center on the land would need a completely new planning application. Kieran Cummins, director of Eco-Advocacy, said at the time: "The permission should have been reassessed in the light of this new landscape."
/data-centers/ireland/county-galway/.unconfirmed: No readable reporting was found of a new data centre planning application in County Galway, or of a sale of the Derrydonnell site after 2022. Search snippets implying a live permission to 2026 came from 2021 stories that the June 2022 High Court order overtook. The 2019 sale listing ('Data Hub West', Binswanger) was not independently read, so it was dropped.

paragraphs: Ireland's national planning appeals body, An Coimisiún Pleanála, refused permission on September 17, 2026, for a data centre outside Killala in north County Mayo, overturning an approval Mayo County Council had granted in April 2025, RTÉ reported. The applicant, Mayo Data Hub Ltd, is part of US-based Avaio Digital, according to The Journal, which put the development at €1.5 billion. The site, at Mullafarry and Tawnaghmore Upper, is 1.8km south of Killala and 10.5km north of Ballina, and the facility was to require 50MW of average electrical power. Mayo Data Hub's application described a 29,000-square-metre facility with a data centre, administrative buildings, electrical and mechanical plant rooms and 56 parking spaces.

The appeal was brought by Colin Doyle, a retired scientist from Ennis, Co Clare, whose objection centred on greenhouse gas emissions and Ireland's climate commitments. In a four-page ruling, the commission said the applicant had failed to show it had a fixed connection agreement to the electricity grid, had not shown the existing infrastructure had enough capacity to power the centre, and had no significant onsite renewable energy, RTÉ reported. The commission found the project would not accord with the Climate Action Plan 2025. It noted wind energy projects near the site but said the developer had provided no evidence it could use locally generated renewable power, according to The Journal. The company had planned backup generators running on fossil gas and biodiesel.

Other objectors when the plans were first lodged included the author Sally Rooney, who lives in Mayo and argued the centre's power demand would add to the "catastrophic planetary crisis that is global warming". Doyle told The Journal he hoped the ruling "represents a change in thinking" about data centres' environmental obligations. Aontú TD Paul Lawless called the refusal "welcome news for Mayo" and said data centres accounted for 22 per cent of electricity used in the State in 2024, the Connaught Telegraph reported. Avaio Digital had told the Western People that about 300 construction jobs and 30 to 35 permanent jobs were expected, The Journal reported. The ruling can be challenged only by judicial review, which must be filed within eight weeks of the decision being formally published.
/data-centers/ireland/county-mayo/.unconfirmed: Did not use Senator Cathal Byrne's claim that the centre would be 'fully provided with electricity off diesel generators' since it conflicts with the ruling's description of grid supply plus backup generators. Irish Times appeal story (May 2025) not read. Whether Avaio will seek judicial review not found.

paragraphs: The largest data center project underway in the Osaka area sits on the old Sharp LCD panel plant in Sakai, south of Osaka city. KDDI bought part of the site and started running its Osaka Sakai Data Center on January 22, 2026, a four-story building finished in about six months, DatacenterDynamics reported. SoftBank bought the rest of the site and is building its own data center there, which it has said could grow to 400 megawatts.

North of the city, Vantage Data Centers is building a two-building, 68-megawatt campus called KIX1; it said in 2024 that the first 28-megawatt building would open in early 2026, but no opening has since been announced. AirTrunk, owned by Blackstone and Canada's CPPIB, runs a 20-megawatt building in nearby Amagasaki and said in December 2025 it plans a second, up to 100 megawatts, in east Osaka, with no delivery date given. No organized local opposition to any of these projects has been reported.
Osaka's other tracked sites, run by Equinix, NTT, Google, MC Digital Realty and CloudHQ, are already operating or under construction in Osaka city and Ibaraki.

Groningen has Google and QTS data centers running and more being built. Google opened its Eemshaven data center in 2018 and a second at Hoogebrug 3 in Winschoten, a €600 million project begun in December 2023, and it broke ground in April 2024 on a third site at the Westpoort industrial estate west of Hoogkerk, in the city of Groningen. QTS, which has owned the EEMSDC1 data center in Eemshaven and one at Zernike Park in Groningen city since 2019, is building a second, much larger building on the Kwelderweg.

QTS says it is investing €1.4 billion in the Eemshaven expansion through 2029 and will need about 130 people to run it. It says its data centers built since 2018 use no water for evaporative cooling, and the new building is prepared for a future district heating link. Google's Winschoten building uses air cooling to cut water use and has solar panels on the roof.

The national government has limited new very large data centers, over 10 hectares with a 70-megawatt grid connection, to two places, and one is the former municipality of Eemsmond, now part of Het Hogeland, which includes the Eemshaven port. The cabinet chose it because it lies at the edge of the country, has room and has enough green power, RTV Noord reported.

The data center activity in Setúbal district centers on Sines, a coastal industrial town about 90 km from Lisbon. There Start Campus is developing the SINES Data Campus, which it says will eventually have six buildings and about 1.2 GW of IT capacity. Only the first building, SIN01, is operating. DCD reported that it launched in January 2025. Start Campus's chief operating officer, Luis Rodrigues, told New Project Media that SIN01 delivers 31 MW and is fully leased, and that the second building, SIN02, will add 180 to 200 MW. The company puts the total projected investment at about EUR 8.5 billion. The campus is designed to cool with seawater rather than freshwater.

The project was at the center of Operation Influencer, the corruption investigation that led Prime Minister António Costa to resign in November 2023. DCD reported that the probe covered a hydrogen plant, several lithium mines and the Start Campus site, and that Start Campus executives were arrested and its premises searched. DCD later reported that charges against former CEO Afonso Salema had been dropped.

The same month, Portugal's Institute for Nature Conservation and Forests (ICNF) found after a November 13 to 17, 2023 inspection that the first building had been built on top of a temporary Mediterranean pond. Protecting that pond was a condition of exempting the first phase, known as NEST, from a full environmental impact assessment. According to the ICNF statement published by Portugal Resident, one of two sites set aside for relocating protected heather had been partially landfilled, and the second had been invaded by exotic species. The institute referred its findings to the Alentejo regional coordination commission, which decides on administrative penalties. Biologist Rita Alcazar of the League for the Protection of Nature said, "the data centre has already been built on top of one of the temporary ponds." Francisco Ferreira of the environmental group ZERO criticized the exemption, arguing that with construction already under way there would be no room for a negative opinion when the later phases came up for assessment. Those phases lie inside the Southwest Coast Special Area of Conservation. Start Campus told DCD that the heather had been moved to a nursery and would be replanted, and that no construction had begun on the later phases.

The campus has since drawn major AI tenants. In October 2025, Microsoft, the AI cloud company Nscale and Start Campus announced a partnership under which Nscale would deploy up to 12,600 Nvidia GB300 chips for Microsoft in Sines. In November 2025, Microsoft president Brad Smith said the company planned to invest $10 billion in AI data centers there. New Project Media reported that Portugal's grid bottleneck is delaying developers, Start Campus among them, though Rodrigues said he welcomed it as a sign of healthy competition.
/data-centers/portugal/setubal/.unconfirmed: Essential Business (EUR 2bn Microsoft deal, March 2026) returned a WordPress error page and was not used. Nscale's May 2026 Rubin GPU expansion and a second 200 MW building appeared only in a company press release and snippet, so they were dropped. The Lisbon Court of Appeal ruling and the EUR 600,000 bond return appeared only in snippets and were dropped. Whether the Alentejo commission imposed any penalty was not found. The site lists SIN01 at 33 MW; the COO interview says 31 MW. The NPM interview is undated.

paragraphs: Microsoft can restart building server halls four and five at its Tuna data center in Sandviken, Gefle Dagblad reported on April 10, 2026, after work stood still for more than a year. Microsoft runs a cluster of data centers between Gävle and Sandviken, at Tuna in Sandviken and at Ersbo and Stackbo in Gävle municipality, with plans for five halls per site. The Sandviken center officially opened in November 2021.

The holdup was power. Vattenfall's three new 145,000-volt lines to Tuna must cross Rörberg, the old Gävle-Sandviken airport, and its permit depended on the airport closing. Gävle's council voted in September 2024 to close it, but a local flying club appealed and sought a referendum, and Microsoft paused Tuna in April 2025. "Det är ingen idé att investera om man inte har ström" (there is no point investing without power), Microsoft energy chief Patrik Öhlund told the paper.

In March 2026 the Supreme Administrative Court declined to hear the club's appeal, making the closure final. A Vattenfall spokesman said the company was now a step closer to connecting its customer. Computer Sweden had reported that even with the airport closed, the new power line would not be finished before 2028 or 2029.

Khazna Data Centers is building QAJ1 in Ajman, a 100-megawatt data center of 20 halls of 5 megawatts each, designed for dense AI chip clusters and cooled by liquid rather than air. The steel structures are complete and the first phase is due to be finished in December 2026, the company said. Power is to come from Etihad Water and Electricity Company.

Khazna announced the site in October 2024 as the largest in its portfolio. In February 2026 it won Uptime Institute Tier III certification for the design, the first stage of that certification; the finished building has not yet been certified. Khazna, part of the Abu Dhabi AI group G42, controls about 70% of the UAE's operating data center capacity, Rest of World reported.

Heat and water are the obvious questions in a desert. "The Ajman site is designed to meet those demands using advanced closed-loop liquid cooling systems and chip-to-chip cooling," chief strategy officer Johan Nilerud told Rest of World.

"We don't want to see it, hear it or smell it," Justice of the Peace Mike Nevens, one of the county judge's advisers, said of the data center proposed outside Sheridan, the Grant County seat. It is being put together by Clean Cloud Energy, an Austin, Texas company that has spent more than a year trying to find an end user for a 753-acre site. Materials presented to the county described a data center needing about 500 megawatts of electricity paired with a solar facility of about 400 megawatts, with combined construction costs estimated at $5 billion to $6 billion. The Arkansas Times reported in July 2026 that the data center plan had grown to 800 megawatts after the Arkansas Electric Cooperative Corp. found additional electricity providers.

In October 2025 the Grant County Quorum Court passed two nonbinding resolutions supporting the data center and the solar farm and letting the county consider payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements with up to a 65% tax abatement. The resolutions do not commit the county to any final agreement, and the court set aside money to hire an attorney to represent the county. Deltaplex News reported in December 2025 that the project had been the subject of legal action since it was first announced. At a later monthly meeting, County Judge Randy Pruitt told justices the project remained on hold because no end user had been confirmed.

At the Quorum Court's July 20, 2026 meeting, Pruitt disclosed, after being asked directly, that EdgeConneX, a data center developer owned by EQT Infrastructure, had signed a letter of intent with Clean Cloud in late June. He said he had been asked to keep the name quiet. "That was fine, but I told them that if someone asked me, I wasn't going to lie and say I didn't know anything," Pruitt told the Arkansas Times. The letter of intent gives EdgeConneX 120 days for due diligence, with an optional 30 more. Pruitt said the county had not negotiated with the company and that Clean Cloud described it as a potential buyer. The Arkansas Times put the project's value at $8 billion to $12 billion.

The county has published the terms it would demand. Nevens went on: "We don't want it to ruin our water table, we don't want it to raise electric rates for our citizens, and we don't want it to ruin our internet." A company meeting those conditions would be considered for a 20% abatement. To reach 65%, Pruitt said, the operator would have to pay close to $57 million up front, including $7.5 million to cut $1,000 from each county property owner's taxes, plus $12.4 million a year on top of the remaining 35% of property taxes. Pruitt said no Grant County official had signed a nondisclosure agreement. According to the Arkansas Times, the proposed closed-loop cooling system would use about as much water a year as a handful of average-sized homes, and electric company officials have said the data center would not by itself cause a rate increase. The paper described the proposal as having at times become an emotional topic in the Sheridan area.
/data-centers/united-states/arkansas/gra.unconfirmed: KARK and FOX16 (KLRT) returned access-denied pages and South Arkansas Reckoning returned only a Ghost shell, so the courthouse protest (and resident quotes such as Brody Channell's) is left out. Arkansas Democrat-Gazette not tried (paywall). Did not find what the legal action mentioned by Deltaplex was, or any news after July 2026. The KTLO republication of the Arkansas Times story was read (counted) but not cited separately.

paragraphs: The one data center moving forward in Connecticut is small. ReNew Developers wants a 15,000-square-foot building on Riverside Avenue in Bristol, on the former Dodge Village site beside the Pequabuck River, powered by a 4-megawatt fuel cell on site. The state Siting Council approved the fuel cell in December 2022, and Bristol's Inland Wetlands Commission approved the project in April 2026. Mayor Ellen Zoppo-Sassu wrote that it would buy city water and use closed-loop cooling, using about 30% of the water of a local grocery store.

The state's largest proposal is gone. NE Edge had planned a campus in Waterford drawing power directly from the Millstone Nuclear Power Station; in April 2026 its host fee agreement with the town ended in default, after nearly three years of opposition from the Concerned Citizens of Waterford and East Lyme. The group used grid operator data showing both Millstone reactors were offline for five weeks to challenge NE Edge's claim that it would not need backup generators.

Towns are acting before projects arrive. Groton adopted a one-year moratorium in 2022 and then zoning that bans data centers over 12,500 square feet, and Morris approved a two-year moratorium in 2026 to protect its farmland. "We can't control that, that's all state jurisdiction. This is something we can control," Morris zoning officer Tony Adili said. New Haven's draft ordinance lists West Haven among the towns that have paused or studied data centers.

In New Haven, Board of Alders Majority Leader Richard Furlow proposed a 12-month moratorium in July; it needs a committee public hearing before a final vote by the full board. The 2026 legislature ended without acting on bills to end the state's data center tax break or to regulate data centers drawing power from a plant such as Millstone.

Delaware's largest data center fight has been over Project Washington, a 1.2-gigawatt campus that Starwood Digital Ventures proposed on land owned by PBF Energy just north of the Delaware City Refinery. In early 2026 Environmental Secretary Greg Patterson ruled that the project was heavy industry and therefore barred by the Coastal Zone Act, the 1971 state law that keeps new heavy industry off Delaware's shoreline. Patterson pointed to the 516 backup diesel generators in the plan and the 2.5 million gallons of stored diesel they would need, which he called "entirely unprecedented." Starwood appealed to the Coastal Zone Industrial Control Board. After about 14 hours of testimony over three days, the board unanimously upheld Patterson's ruling on March 26, 2026, Spotlight Delaware reported.

Starwood then appealed to Delaware Superior Court but quietly withdrew that appeal in early July 2026, two days after the legislature passed a package of stricter data center bills. With no other challenge pending, Spotlight Delaware reported in August, the project cannot go ahead in its current design. Starwood spokesman Jim Lamb said the company "is continuing its work with state and local regulators, labor, and the entire community to find a pathway forward." Dustyn Thompson of Sierra Club Delaware warned that because the Coastal Zone Act does not name data centers, developers could try coastal sites again.

Gov. Matt Meyer signed those bills in late August 2026. WHYY reported that the law bars data centers from passing the cost of powering and upgrading their facilities on to other ratepayers. It directs Delmarva Power to create a separate, higher rate for hyperscale data centers and requires them to cut power use at peak demand. A separate law requires data centers to generate their own power over a 10-year period from sources that meet the state's renewable portfolio standards, and another bars them from job-creation tax credits. "Data centers that do not pay their fair share do not belong in our communities," Meyer said. WHYY noted that a state report found data center demand could push average wholesale electricity prices up by more than 80%.

Counties have also acted. On March 10, 2026, New Castle County Council unanimously passed Councilmember David Carter's ordinance, the county's first zoning rules for data centers, after seven months of debate, Delaware Public Media reported. It requires a 1,000-foot buffer from residential zones, schools and day cares, which can shrink to 500 feet with a site-specific noise study, and it bans open-loop cooling. An amendment limited the rules to applications filed after enactment, which exempted Project Washington. Kent County Levy Court unanimously adopted its own rules in July 2026, with 300-foot residential buffers, a noise limit, and required letters from water and electric providers. The rules apply only to unincorporated areas, not to cities like Harrington, where a data center had been eyed at the former Burris Logistics site. Kent's attorney said the county is reviewing whether a full ban would be legally viable.

Two other New Castle County proposals are still unresolved. Near Newark, developer Shelbourne filed plans in 2025 to replace the White Clay Center buildings with a three-building, roughly 850,000-square-foot data center campus. Councilman Tim Sheldon said in June 2026 that he had brokered a handshake deal with the developer's attorney to pause it. Spotlight Delaware noted that the agreement is not binding, depends on the county approving an exploratory plan that would grandfather the site under the old rules, and leaves the developer free to build a data center later. A separate proposal near St. Georges, on land that includes the Frightland Halloween attraction, was still in preliminary stages in August 2026 and also sits inside the coastal zone.

Frightland acreage and zoning details (1,362 acres, 3.24 million sq ft) came from search snippets and were not used. paragraphs: Citrus County's fight over data centers centered on Deltona Corporation's applications for the Holder Industrial Park, a comprehensive plan amendment and zoning change that could have opened the way for a data center near the city of Hernando and the community of Holder. Spectrum News Bay News 9 reported that the request would have converted almost 800 additional acres of agricultural and residential land to industrial use, expanding the park from about 557 acres to a little more than 1,300 acres and re-designating it for heavy industrial use. DatacenterDynamics described the combined footprint as around 1,400 acres and noted that Deltona is primarily known as a homebuilder.

On May 13, 2026, the Board of County Commissioners agreed to impose a moratorium of no more than 12 months covering building permits, development orders and rezonings tied to data centers, with a formal ordinance to follow at the board's next meeting, Bay News 9 reported. Among those opposed was farm owner April Bulla, who lives a few miles from the proposed site near County Road 491 and Tram Road in Lecanto and said developers seem to target rural communities "that sit on top of the aquifer." "If you allow a data center to be built here in Citrus County, people will not forget that," resident Tracy Landry told commissioners. "Personally, I'm a nature girl," said Commissioner Holly Davis. "I grew up here; I don't want them here." Commissioner Jeff Kinnard said the county needed "an ordinance on the book that is specific to data centers to protect our environment, to protect our neighbors," and called the staff draft then headed to the planning board incomplete.

Because Deltona had filed before the moratorium took effect, its application still had to be heard. On June 18, 2026, the county's Planning and Development Commission voted it down. "That's not where heavy industrial goes so definitely there are concerns about that," said Joanna Coutu, the county's director of land development and deputy growth manager, describing the surrounding low-density residential, rural residential and agricultural land. An attorney for the applicant, Clark Stillwell, argued that residents' concerns about noise, vibration and water relied on outdated examples. The planning board's vote was not the last word; the county commission had public hearings set for July 14.

Those hearings never happened. According to DatacenterDynamics, the company sent the county a formal notice withdrawing both applications on Tuesday, June 23, 2026, a day after commissioners voted to deny its request to delay a decision. FOX 13 reported that the county canceled the July 14 hearings, that the one-year moratorium remains in effect, and that the county is still working on an ordinance to regulate future data center proposals. Florida's new state data center law, which DatacenterDynamics said bars utilities from passing infrastructure costs on to consumers, took effect on July 1, 2026.
/data-centers/united-states/florida/citr.unconfirmed: Florida Politics (browser wall, two stories) and WFLA (access denied) not readable. Dropped: exact adoption date and vote count of the moratorium ordinance (only the May 13, 2026 agreement is sourced; the site record's May 26, 2026 start date was not confirmed in an article I read). The Bay News 9 May 13 story places the proposed site near County Road 491 and Tram Road in Lecanto, and DCD places the 798-acre parcel between North Lecanto Highway, North Tram Road and North Florida Avenue; I treated these as the same Deltona/Holder project. The site's separate 'Deltona Corporation, Citrus County' and 'Hernando Deltona Data Center' entries appear to describe this one project.

paragraphs: Orange County commissioners agreed on September 15, 2026 to pursue a temporary moratorium of six to 18 months on new data centers, before any company has applied to build a large one. Staff must now write the ordinance, and a vote is expected at the board's December 1 meeting. The data center under construction in the county is HostDime's seven-story, 100,000-square-foot building along I-4 near Lee Road in the Town of Eatonville, which could open in October if it passes final inspection.

Commissioner Kelly Martinez Semrad, who proposed the pause, said the county's code has no reference to data centers at all, and that she received more than 800 emails in favor of a moratorium. Of the 54 people registered to speak at the September meeting, none said they wanted to live next to one. "A moratorium gives the county time to choose the rules," she said. State Rep. Anna Eskamani and Susannah Randolph of Sierra Club Florida also spoke for it.

Water is the main worry. Martinez Semrad said the county faces a 96-million-gallon-a-day water shortfall by 2045, and that the largest data centers can use up to 5 million gallons a day. "Water is a finite resource, and we know that our aquifer is already strained as it is," said county chief planner Marcus Bastian. Florida law defines a large data center as one using 50 megawatts of power or more; county staff said smaller ones of 2 to 5 megawatts have operated here for decades.

HostDime broke ground in Eatonville in 2016 on a smaller building meant to open in 2018. Since missing its July 2025 deadline it has owed the town $250 a day, $99,250 by September 1, 2026. The Town Council put off a vote on doubling the fine so it could meet the company first, and Mayor Ruthi Critton said the town still wants the data center to open.

Warner Robins has put data centers on hold. On July 20, 2026, the city council approved a six-month moratorium on data center applications, which runs through January 20, 2027, according to WGXA and 41NBC. Mayor LaRhonda Patrick said the city will use the pause to study effects on water, electricity, gas, zoning, property values and residential rates, and to hold listening sessions with residents. "We can't allow someone to come in and suck up all our water resources, and be left with water with low pressure, for example," Patrick told 41NBC. "That's what we're hearing in other communities." She told WGXA the city would consult experts on "what's really happening when it comes to the water table, when it comes to the sewer, when it comes to the electric grid."

The one data center project tracked in the county is a proposal to lease federal land at Robins Air Force Base, next to Warner Robins. On October 15, 2025, the Department of the Air Force asked private companies for proposals to lease underused land for AI data centers at five bases, including three sites of between 30 and 135 acres at Robins, according to DatacenterDynamics and Air & Space Forces Magazine. Under President Trump's Executive Order 14318, each project had to involve at least $500 million in capital spending and more than 100 megawatts of power. Leases could run up to 50 years, and offers were due November 14, 2025. The notice said lessees must obtain and pay for "any and all utilities, including but not limited to power and water" at their own cost, and that the service would favor proposals that keep utilities for the base and the surrounding community accessible and affordable. The Air Force was scheduled to select applicants in January 2026; no result has been published.

The Social Circle City Council approved a data center planned by Carrollton-based Atlas Development on 151 acres at Hawkins Academy Road and Roy Malcom Road in November 2025. In a series of 2-1 votes, the council approved annexation, rezoning from agricultural to light industrial, a special-use permit and a land-use map change, despite the planning commission's recommendation to deny each request. The project totals nearly 1.5 million square feet of buildings and an electrical substation, with conditions including single-story buildings and a reversion to agricultural zoning if construction has not begun within three years.

Residents packed the vote, with most objections coming from people living outside the city limits in unincorporated Walton County. "We don't have a voting voice on this council that votes these projects in," said Christina Studdard. One resident described rising bills: "Five years ago, my electricity was $114 per month... Now, it's $193." Mike Owens, who lives across the street and sits on the area's joint development authority, said data centers belong in industrial parks, not on zoning "islands."

The only data center already operating near Social Circle is Meta's, at the Stanton Springs development just outside the city limits. Social Circle paused new data center applications for six months starting September 2025, then in early 2026 adopted rules requiring special-use permits, a 50-acre minimum lot, noise limits, and water, sewer and gas impact studies for any future proposal.

In April 2025 Kosciusko County, in northern Indiana, rejected the only data center it has faced, and not one local official voted for it. Prologis, the San Francisco-based industrial real estate company, asked to rezone about 554 acres of farmland north of County Road 700 N and west of CR 300 W, about three miles northwest of Leesburg, from agricultural to industrial (Industrial-3). It planned to build a data center and lease it to a tenant it had not named. Prologis Senior Vice President JC Witt said the company chose the site because three power transmission lines converge there, near a NIPSCO substation. The landowners agreed that the land, if rezoned, could be used only for a data center.

The county's Area Plan Commission voted 8-0 on April 2, 2025 to recommend denial. That vote was advisory, and the final decision belonged to the three county commissioners. WSBT reported that the meeting was packed, with about 100 more people watching from an annex and more than 350 online, and a petition against the project gathered more than a thousand signatures. Plan Commission President Lee Hardman worried that approval would lead to more development around it: "I think it opens a Pandora's box that I'm not comfortable with at all." Residents raised the loss of productive farmland, water and power use, traffic, and the effect on the area's Amish farming community. A representative of Kosciusko REMC, the county's electric cooperative, said the project would not raise rates or strain the co-op's supply.

The commissioners voted unanimously on April 22, 2025 to deny the rezoning. "The rezoning of property should be denied because it is not a reasonable and prudent location for this type of development," Commissioner Sue Ann Mitchell said before her vote. Witt told the board the company would not look elsewhere in the county: "it's not going to be another location." Local attorney Jack Birch argued that Prologis could instead extend power lines to a less objectionable site.

Estimates of the tax revenue varied widely. Inside INdiana Business reported that Prologis projected about $355 million in property taxes over 20 years, compared with a little over $350,000 if the land stayed in farming. DCD reported a Prologis estimate of $35.8 million over 20 years. When DCD reported the denial in April 2025, the county had no data centers. Afterward, Prologis said that because of the one-year wait before it could reapply, it did not plan to keep pursuing the project.

paragraphs: Shelbyville's Common Council approved a Prologis data center campus on April 6, 2026, against its own Plan Commission's advice, in a meeting moved to the high school auditorium to fit the crowd. The project annexes about 575 acres at the State Road 44/I-74 interchange for up to 11 buildings; no tenant has been named. In exchange for at least $2 billion in spending and 25 jobs per building, the council also approved a 30-year full tax abatement on equipment and a 10-year half abatement on real property.

The Plan Commission had recommended against the rezoning in January, and hundreds of residents packed a hearing to protest, warning about farmland loss and water use. Connie Lindsay, who organized Shelbyville Citizens Against Data Centers, said more than 6,700 people had signed the group's petition. "The environmental issues, health and safety issues, we're losing valuable farm ground," she told WRTV. The council's final vote, 4-2-1, went ahead anyway; one member abstained because his law firm represents Prologis.

Separately, Shelby County commissioners adopted a six-month moratorium on data centers in unincorporated parts of the county while a separate ordinance was drafted; it does not apply to the annexed Prologis site. The county's plan commission aimed to send its recommendation in time for a commissioners' vote before the moratorium expired: the vote was scheduled for August 23, 2026, and no result has been published.

Alcove Development of Lawrence is proposing Project Catalyst, a data center campus of 500 megawatts of power or more on a 283-acre site inside Osawatomie city limits, near West 335th Street and Osawatomie Road. As of mid-September the Osawatomie Planning Commission was weighing whether to recommend it to the City Council, which makes the decision. The county's three-year moratorium on data centers covers only unincorporated land, so it does not apply here.

The city has agreed to waive half the project's property taxes for 10 years and to supply 80,000 gallons of water a day for cooling, which City Manager Bret Glendening says is about 10 percent of the plant's usual output. Officials project $30 million a year for the city and $10 million each for Miami County and the school district. "This is huge," Glendening said. The city says the campus will be air-cooled and that Evergy's rates for very large customers keep its power costs off homeowners' bills.

Many neighbors are opposed. A summer City Council meeting ran four hours, with worries about water, power and noise for patients at Osawatomie State Hospital nearby. Troy Harp, who leads the opposition, said Alcove's own plans point to a natural gas power plant; an earlier petition against the project was ruled invalid, and in June he began collecting signatures for a new one to limit its size. "The billionaires know how to play these country towns," resident Michael Hursey said.

For about three years a bitcoin mine has run inside Hopkinsville Electric System's Holland Substation on North Campbell Street, largely outside public view, the Hoptown Chronicle reported in July 2026. The operation, about 22 modular units drawing roughly 15 megawatts, is owned by North Campbell Land Co., which was part of Cathedra until Cathedra became a wholly owned subsidiary of the Nasdaq-listed Sphere 3D in a transaction approved in June 2026. It came to light at a late-July public hearing held by Hopkinsville's Community and Development Services on the city's first data center zoning rules.

At that hearing the company outlined two plans: converting the existing 15-megawatt mine from bitcoin to other computing work, and building a second, 50-megawatt data center at another site in the city. Company representatives said North Campbell would pay the estimated $8 million to $10 million cost of a new 65-megawatt HES substation, with 15 megawatts left for other HES customers. DCD reported in August 2026 that the second site's location, footprint, cost and schedule had not been disclosed and that no AI or HPC customers had been announced. HES general manager Jeff Hurd said revenue from the mine helps the utility avoid rate increases for its 13,000 customers, and later told city council members that TVA could supply the added power without affecting existing customers.

The draft rules dated July 17 would sort data centers by load and footprint and ban "hyper-scale" facilities of 75 megawatts or more or 50,000 square feet or more. Large-scale centers would need a 1,000-foot setback from residential, public and quasi-public property. The existing mine would likely be grandfathered. Attorneys for HES and North Campbell called the setbacks too restrictive, and HES submitted its own alternative ordinance. "Make no mistake, if you adopt the more restrictive ordinance, you will effectively ban data centers in the city of Hopkinsville," said Robert Ison, the company's attorney.

Nineteen people spoke. NCLC representative Thomas Masiero said that "there has not been a noise or water complaint against our facility during the three years of operation," and that the mine takes part in a flexible-load program that can cut its power use quickly. Most residents who spoke asked for protections for the environment and community health. Pembroke resident Sherry Byerline said, "Once they get in and get a foothold, they pretty much do what they want to do, and this creates continuous pollution." Hopkinsville resident Becca Hostilo asked that closed-loop water systems be required and said, "I would also like to suggest we have a cap on the number of centers that may come into this town." A second CDS hearing is set for 6 p.m. Monday, Sept. 28, 2026, at Hopkinsville Community College. CDS will then send a proposed ordinance to the Hopkinsville City Council, which has the final say.

Kentucky New Era (paywall) and WHOP not read. Christian County Fiscal Court has no data center action on the record in anything I read; the regulations discussed are Hopkinsville city zoning.

paragraphs: Middlesex County's data center fight is in Lowell, where Markley Group runs the state's largest data center, a 352,000-square-foot building on the old Prince spaghetti factory site. In August 2026 a Middlesex Superior Court judge temporarily blocked Markley from installing four new diesel backup generators, while letting it run four it had already put in. Residents had sued the state Department of Environmental Protection in April over its approval of a plan for 27 diesel generators on the site.

Lowell's City Council passed a one-year moratorium on new data centers or expansions in March 2026, but Markley challenged it and in July reached a deal with the city letting it go ahead with expansion plans filed before the pause. "The moratorium is essentially null and void. It affects future data centers but not this one," resident Sienna Herbert told GBH. State Sen. Vanna Howard of Lowell has told the Senate that some neighbors' electric bills rose more than 50% and described exhaust in bedrooms and noise at night.

In Everett, where no data center has been proposed, the City Council on June 22, 2026 limited any data center in the Docklands Innovation District to 20,000 square feet or five megawatts of power, whichever is smaller, with a special permit. Equinix also runs an established data center campus in Billerica.

The main data center fight in Wright County is in Monticello, where Monticello Tech LLC, a group tied to developer Nick Frattalone, wants to build a campus of up to 3 million square feet on about 550 acres south of 85th Street and east of Highway 25. The site is in Monticello Township but inside an orderly annexation area that allows it to be annexed into the city. A second developer, Scannell Properties, has floated four buildings on about 106 acres near Otter Creek and the Bertram Chain of Lakes Regional Park.

On April 27, 2026, the Monticello City Council voted 4-1 to adopt a Data Center Planned Unit Development ordinance, with council member Charlotte Gabler voting no. The ordinance creates a zoning district for data centers. Developers must get a rezoning and then a conditional use permit, show there is enough water and energy, and meet standards for buffers, noise and lighting. The council raised the minimum setback from homes to 300 feet, which opponents said was not enough. MPR News reported that the ordinance also rules out city tax incentives and makes developers pay for any new infrastructure. About a dozen people spoke at the meeting, nearly all opposed. Jenna Van Den Boom, an organizer of Stop the Monticello Data Centers, called the vote "a kick in the gut." Mayor Lloyd Hilgart said, "I believe that everything but the kitchen sink is in that ordinance."

Monticello Tech filed its formal applications for a conditional use permit, rezoning and preliminary plat on July 6, 2026. The city found them incomplete, and a revised submission in August was ruled complete. The Monticello Times reported that the filing describes up to eight buildings on about 547 acres, built in phases over four to eight years. It estimates about 75,000 gallons of water a day using dry cooling and about $45.9 million in public infrastructure that the applicant says the developer or the eventual operator would pay for. No end user has been named. Electricity use is not quantified. Xcel Energy would serve the site through a new substation on its 345-kilovolt system, with transmission upgrades at the developer's expense. The Planning Commission, which is advisory only, has a public hearing set for October 6, 2026, and the city says it must decide by December 8, 2026.

The Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy sued Monticello in Wright County District Court in February 2026, arguing that the city's Alternative Urban Areawide Review of the site did not adequately evaluate environmental impacts. Under an agreement between the parties, Monticello Tech can keep pursuing permits but must give 90 days' written notice before any grading or site work. A pretrial conference is set for December 29.

Outside the cities, the Wright County Board of Commissioners unanimously approved an emergency moratorium on May 19, 2026. County Ordinance 26-2 pauses applications to build data centers in all of the county's 18 townships, including townships that do their own planning and zoning, and gives the county up to one year to study the issue and adopt rules on the time, place and manner in which data centers would be allowed. Fourteen people spoke at the public hearing, all in favor of the moratorium. Commissioner Kirby Moynagh said the county needed to be "proactive instead of reactive." Board Chair Darek Vetsch cautioned that the pause is not a ban: "If you create an ordinance that says you shall not build a data center in Wright County, we will get litigated and we will lose." The moratorium does not change Monticello's ordinance.
/data-centers/united-states/minnesota/wr.unconfirmed: KRWC says the moratorium gives the county 'up to one year'; no exact end date was in the text read. The 'Project Groundhog' name and Microsoft as the tenant (from a snippet about a November 18 rezoning) were not confirmed in any text read and were dropped. The Frattalone link rests on the Monticello Times photo caption naming 'Monticello Tech representatives, including developer Nick Frattalone'.

paragraphs: Madison County is home to both of Amazon Web Services' first Mississippi data center campuses, one outside Canton and one in Ridgeland. As of June 2026 the Canton campus was the only one of Amazon's four announced Mississippi facilities in operation; Ridgeland, Clinton and Vicksburg were still in the works, Mississippi Today reported. An Amazon spokesperson, David Ross, told the outlet that the company had five buildings operating at Canton "with plans to at least double that presence," and that the Ridgeland site was "in the early stages of construction." Statewide, Amazon says it plans to invest $25 billion and create 2,000 jobs.

Money has become the main point of friction at the county level. Madison County has fee-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements with Amazon for both campuses, and part of the revenue is going toward repaying a $215 million state infrastructure loan tied to the data centers. Even so, the county's share is projected to climb to $16.5 million by 2029 and $29 million by 2031, the Mississippi Free Press reported. At an Aug. 17, 2026 meeting, the Board of Supervisors upheld Tax Assessor Norman Cannady's valuation of about $292 million for each of the five operating Canton buildings, rejecting Amazon's appeal, which put the value at about $69 million per building. The assessor's office estimated the lower figure would have cost the county $5.8 million in revenue this fiscal year. Cannady said Amazon had declined repeated requests for its construction costs: "They were not willing to share any of that with us." Amazon can still contest the valuation in court, and Cannady said the company could push for lower values in later years as more buildings come online.

Water for the campuses has been a recurring public question. Amazon said the Canton site currently draws cooling water from Canton Municipal Utilities and plans, with the contractor Veolia, to switch to recycled wastewater from the Madison County Wastewater Authority. A Veolia executive, Chris Low, estimated Canton would use about 83 million gallons of recycled wastewater a year. In Ridgeland, Amazon said it will use water only from the city system, up to about 93 million gallons a year, and that it is putting $37 million into that system. The company says it will use water for cooling only about 9% of the year and rely on air cooling the rest of the time. These figures come from the company and its contractor and have not been independently published.

The power arrangements are largely out of public view. Both campuses are served by Entergy Mississippi, and under a 2024 law passed in a special legislative session the Amazon-Entergy contract took effect without approval from the Public Service Commission, which is barred from altering its terms for the contract's full, undisclosed length. The law also lets Entergy begin recovering construction costs before facilities are in service and removes a 4% cap on annual rate increases tied to the Amazon spending. Entergy projects that by 2030 its rates will be 16% lower than they otherwise would have been, but, as Mississippi Today reported in June 2026, that claim cannot be checked because the contract is confidential. "It is the worst piece of legislation I think I have ever seen in my entire time watchdogging the utility industry," said Daniel Tait of the Energy & Policy Institute. Harvard's Ari Peskoe said, "I can't think of another state law passed by a legislature that exempts a specific contract from regulatory review."

Left out Prado AI's proposed self-powered Ridgeland campus: I read the April 2026 filing story, but search snippets say the developer later moved the site to an unnamed Jackson-metro location and the PSC declined to rule, and I did not read those follow-ups. Also left out the 2024 announcement dollar and acreage figures (search snippets only) and the July 2026 loan-paydown vote (WLBT not read).

paragraphs: Starkville's Planning and Zoning Commission voted on August 11, 2026 against a bitcoin mining facility at 407 Industrial Park Road, after more than 80 residents packed City Hall to oppose it. The Board of Aldermen was scheduled to take up the decision on August 18; no result has been published. If the board denies it, the developer can appeal in court or reapply next year, and its representative, Mandy Jiang of Starkville Energy LLC, said: "We're probably going to appeal."

The site is zoned industrial, but crypto mining is not a listed use in the city's development code, so the project needed a special exemption. City planners recommended denial because the application left out water and wastewater needs, employment, flood planning and environmental review. "I've never had an applicant that had such a contentious issue be so unprepared," Commissioner Jeremiah Dumas said. Residents, a Mississippi State professor who owns neighboring land and the next-door Oktibbeha County Humane Society raised noise concerns.

The mine would draw up to 30 megawatts of power, making it Starkville Utilities' second-largest electric customer after Mississippi State University; the developer would pay about $800,000 for transmission lines. Water estimates rose from 20,000 gallons a day in June to about 73,000 at peak, Jiang said in August. Mayor Lynn Spruill backed the project, saying its revenue could spare ratepayers an electric rate increase.

The only data center proposal tracked in Buchanan County, Missouri, a four-building campus on Southeast Pickett Road on the edge of St. Joseph, was withdrawn in June 2026 after weeks of public opposition, and the city has since paused all new data center applications for a year.

Capstone Technology Campus, a company owned by local businessman Steve Craig, had asked St. Joseph to annex a 130-acre parcel at 6321 Pickett Road and to rezone that parcel and 5701 Pickett Road for the project, DatacenterDynamics and KQ2 reported. At a May 27, 2026 city council hearing on the annexation, most speakers objected to the lack of information about how the land would be used. Once the city confirmed that the intended user was a data center, known as STJ Data Center LLC, opposition grew. "In the research I've done, it shows it can affect water quality and water quantities a lot," resident Brandon Strain told KQ2 in June. Project leaders said the campus would employ up to 200 people. According to a draft city fact sheet cited by DatacenterDynamics, the data center would have been developed by Atmosphere Data Centers, and the draft site plan showed four buildings and a substation. Two petitions against the project had gathered more than 720 and 1,500 signatures.

On June 26, 2026, Craig withdrew both the annexation and rezoning applications before the Planning Commission could take them up at its July 23 meeting. "We thought that while this debate is going on and underway, we would pause the situation and evaluate other options as well," Craig told KQ2. The city also canceled a July 16 town hall with the developer and utility providers and said any future proposal would require new applications.

On July 20, 2026, the St. Joseph City Council voted 8-0 for an emergency ordinance suspending new data center projects for 12 months, a length proposed by council member Gary Wilkinson. During the pause, retained experts are to recommend zoning standards, infrastructure considerations, operational requirements and community benefit expectations. Many residents had asked for an 18-month moratorium. "We prefer 18 months, obviously, but 12 months we're overjoyed," said resident Conni Muff, who told KQ2 the concerns all along had been "our water, our electricity, the noise pollution and the light pollution." On August 17, 2026, the council voted 3-6 against a resolution from council member Russell Moore to create a citizens data center advisory committee; Moore, Wilkinson and Collin Clibon voted for it, and Mayor Larry Miller and five council members voted against. Council member Randy Schultz said the council should "take this on ourselves," and KQ2 reported that the opposition group was "shocked and angry" at the outcome.

A Yahoo/The Cool Down rewrite of KQTV reporting on the July 13 work session was read but not used as a source (aggregator); the council's August trip to an Iowa data center town was not read. The News-Press (newspressnow.com) stories were not read.

paragraphs: In Douglas County the data center question is electricity. Nebraska Public Media reported in December 2025 that data centers used 1% of the electricity sold by the Omaha Public Power District in 2018 and 21% in 2024, and are projected to reach 41% by 2035. OPPD has been adding gas-fired generation at Turtle Creek in Sarpy County and in Cass County. The same month, the OPPD board approved an average 6.3% rate increase for 2026, including 6% for residential customers and 8.9% for industrial customers. It also extended operations at the North Omaha Station, where two units still burn coal, while adding planning steps toward their eventual retirement and conversion. Nebraska Public Media reported that OPPD retail rates will have risen about 20% since 2021. OPPD chief financial officer Brad Underwood denied that data center demand is driving up residential rates, saying the utility's cost-of-service method is meant to "make sure that cost-causers are cost- payers."

Douglas County's main data center is Google's campus on the northwest edge of Omaha, near State Street and Blair High Road. Google announced it in April 2022 with a planned $750 million investment. Documents filed with the City of Omaha under the name Westwood Solutions, LLC described about four buildings totaling more than 1.4 million square feet, according to DCD. At the time it was Google's third facility in the Omaha area, after Papillion in neighboring Sarpy County and Council Bluffs across the river in Iowa.

Google paid to speed up road work around the site. Douglas County engineer Todd Pfitzer told the Omaha World-Herald that Google was paying for culvert work on State Street and a three-lane widening toward Blair High Road, and for an extension of 120th Street north to Rainwood Road. The county had estimated the work would cost about $5 million. "Google couldn't wait the six or eight years it would take for the county to get to this," Pfitzer said. State Street runs through the rapidly growing suburbs between northwest Omaha and Bennington.
/data-centers/united-states/nebraska/dou.unconfirmed: The operating date of the Google Omaha campus (a snippet said 2024) was not confirmed in text read, so it was dropped. The site's 237 MW figure is not confirmed. The Omaha World-Herald road story's date is not visible in the text (its URL suggests 2024), so it is written without a date. A Grist/Flatwater story on a Google-Tenaska gas plant concerns southeast Nebraska (Otoe County), not Douglas County, and was not used. One search ('Douglas County Nebraska data center rezoning vote Valley Elkhorn Bennington') returned only Douglas County, Georgia results. No Douglas County rezoning fight or moratorium was found. A fourth search, on the North Omaha coal plant and data centers, was refused because the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted.

paragraphs: Lancaster County's one operating data center is Google's campus north and west of the 56th Street exit on Interstate 80 in north Lincoln. The Lincoln Journal Star reported in 2026 that the site is effectively online for Lincoln Electric System even without a public launch. "For our purposes, the switch has been flipped," said Scott Benson, LES director of strategy and innovation. According to the utility's budget, Google accounts for 11%, or about $41.6 million, of LES's projected 2026 retail revenue. It buys power at Southwest Power Pool market prices rather than standard retail rates, and it is paying for 423 megawatts of wind energy to cover its load. LES put a 3% rate increase in its 2026 budget and is funding two natural gas combustion turbines at the Terry Bundy Generation Station. Benson said the contract was negotiated so existing customers would not carry added risk, but he said details could not be disclosed. The Lincoln Water System supplies the site's cooling water, and a city spokesperson called its consumption private customer information. In December 2025 Google's land company, Agate LLC, filed a $32 million building permit for another structure zoned as a data center.

The current fight is in and around the village of Hallam in the southern part of the county. Monolith, which makes carbon black at its Olive Creek plant there, is proposing a 35-megawatt co-located data center with the Denver company Crusoe, along with four more carbon black units. At a packed town hall in July 2026, Monolith said the data center would be made up of as many as 36 modular Spark units, each about the size of a shipping container, on roughly 10 acres. The company estimated the data center would use about 770,000 gallons of water a year. Residents raised concerns about noise, light and water. "What we've been able to see, and everybody that's come out here, is nothing has been transparent, and everything gets signed, everything gets voted through, and then nothing is what it seems," said landowner Cami Slauson.

Hallam's planning commission delayed its recommendation on August 19, 2026, after a public hearing where, Nebraska Public Media reported, the only resident to speak in favor was a Monolith employee. Tom Hanna, a member of the opposition group Hallam Says No, told the board that data centers were not a contemplated use in the village's comprehensive plan. On September 16, 2026, the commission voted unanimously to recommend a special use permit. That vote is a recommendation, not the final decision: the Hallam Village Board is scheduled to vote at its October 5 meeting. Crusoe said the conditions of approval now include a community benefit agreement whose funds three members of the village would control. Commissioner Cynthia Heier voted yes but said, "I mean, this portion of Nebraska is under attack from big companies who just think we're just throwaway people."

A much larger project may be coming to the land around Hallam. In August 2026 Nebraska Public Media reported that Stark Power, a Tel Aviv developer that bought Sagebrush Infrastructure in June, holds purchase agreements with thirteen landowners for more than 1,400 acres outside Hallam. The agreements were signed between December 2025 and mid-March 2026, and company documents point to a 1.7-gigawatt hyperscale campus next to Nebraska Public Power District's Princeton Road Station, a gas plant set to begin operating in 2029. NPPD confirmed that Stark had applied and signed a memorandum of understanding to begin its New Load Process. A Stark vice president said no final decision had been made. Separately, the Flatwater Free Press reported in March 2026 that Tenaska had optioned at least 450 acres in Lancaster County as part of land gathering across southeast Nebraska, tied in private utility documents to a possible Google data center of 1,000 to 3,000 megawatts powered by a private gas plant.

Commissioner Matt Schulte proposed a county moratorium, but the Lancaster County Board dropped the idea on September 10, 2026, and set up two task forces instead: one on data centers, covering energy and water, and one on industrial zoning. That followed a zoning text amendment filed by Bold Education, tied to Bold Nebraska. Its draft would allow data centers with conditions, including closed-loop or air-cooled systems unless a developer gets special approval. Commissioner Sean Flowerday argued a moratorium was unnecessary because data centers can only go on industrial land and little such land exists in the county. "The truth is there already is an effective moratorium in Lancaster County because you only build these things on industrial land," he said. Schulte, who agreed to drop the moratorium, added, "we are not opposed to data centers." Commissioners told KOLN they hope to have a plan in place by the end of 2026.
