The Flatwater date (March 2026) comes from its 'As of March 11' land-records line and KOLN's March 13, 2026 repost URL. I left out the 141 MW figure on the site's project page because no source I read confirmed it. I did not report the outcome of the October 5 village board vote because it is still in the future. I did not read the Journal Star story on Stark's 1,700 acres or the Beatrice Daily Sun piece.

paragraphs: Reno, Washoe County's largest city, has stopped accepting, processing or approving new data center applications until August 31, 2027, or until it adopts data center rules, whichever comes first. The City Council voted 6-1 on June 1, 2026 to extend a 30-day pause it first passed in May; Councilmember Kathleen Taylor voted no both times. Projects already approved or under construction are not affected, including the Webb and Oppidan data centers in the North Valleys.

Both were approved in early 2025. The Webb Data Center is set to use 28.5 megawatts of power; Oppidan, next to it at North Virginia Street and Stead Boulevard, is set to use 8 megawatts and was approved on appeal after the Planning Commission denied it over water and power. The commission then asked the council to pause approvals, and a proposal for minimum data center standards failed. At the nine-hour June meeting, most public comments called for the pause or a full ban, while construction union members opposed it.

Councilmember Devon Reese, who asked for the pause while running for mayor, said, "No moratorium can be lifted in the absence of regulations." Councilmember Meghan Ebert pushed to tie its end to new rules: "I need to show my community that they will be protected, and that this isn't a political stunt." The council also voted unanimously to start writing data center permit rules.

Wider rules for Reno, Sparks and Washoe County are being studied by the Truckee Meadows Regional Planning Agency, which cannot adopt them itself; local and state governments decide. Its public survey drew more than 9,000 responses by mid-August, 96 percent against data centers. Director Jeremy Smith hopes to present a final report at the regional planning board's October 8 meeting and said he would "make sure that the concept of a ban is loud and clear."

Hunterdon County's only data center project is a small one in the Town of Clinton. Comcast Cable is converting the vacant former TD Bank branch at 92 W. Main Street into a building for computer servers and network equipment, after the town's land use board approved the plan in the summer of 2025. It is a one-story, 2,170-square-foot building on just over an acre that had sat empty for eight to ten years.

The site will not be staffed full time. Comcast will install two generators and remove the drive-through lane at the back of the property; online listings show the building dates from around 1975 and was last renovated around 2017. Comcast also has an office and data center on Centerton Road in Moorestown, in Burlington County.

Otsego County's data center fight has played out in the Town of Oneonta, where a startup called Eco-Yotta Inc. applied to rezone 357 County Highway 9, in the town's West End, from residential-agricultural use to a planned development district that could allow a data center. The request was first announced in July 2025. At an Oct. 8, 2025 town board meeting attended by more than 60 people, AllOtsego reported, Eco-Yotta's representatives said the proposal was no longer a "data center" but a utility used for agriculture, with heat from computers in a 10,000-square-foot barn used to grow crops. Residents raised water use and pollution, noise and light, abandonment of the facility and higher electric bills. Will Rivera, then a candidate for town supervisor, told the board, "Someone pays and it's never the developer; it's the people." The board tabled the application pending more information.

Rivera won the supervisor's seat. On Feb. 11, 2026 the town board voted 3-2 against scheduling a public hearing on a one-year moratorium drafted by the town attorney. Board members Joe Camarata, Brett Holleran and Teresa DeSantis said they had received the draft only minutes before the meeting; Rivera and Deputy Supervisor Patricia Riddell Kent voted in favor. Resident Georgia B. Smith submitted a petition with about 680 signatures supporting a moratorium. The board took the measure up again in March, held a public hearing on April 8, and in May 2026 voted unanimously for a 12-month moratorium on AI data centers and commercial crypto mining, WBNG reported. "We had over 700 of our constituents who submitted the petition to us sharing that they do not approve of these kinds of facilities to being developed," Rivera said. He said the board hopes to ban data centers after the moratorium runs out, and at a March committee meeting he had argued for denying the zone change outright.

The City of Oneonta, which is separate from the town, began drafting its own moratorium in spring 2026. Council member Scott Harrington said the city should adopt one for at least a year, and council members named water use as a main concern, The Daily Star reported. Separately, in November 2025 AllOtsego reported that two unnamed companies had asked Otsego Now, the county development agency, about building a data center at the Oneonta Rail Yards. Otsego Now CEO Jody Zakrevsky called the ideas "not viable" with the site's current infrastructure, noting "very limited gas, if any" and that the electric service "would have to be completely upgraded."
/data-centers/united-states/new-york/ots.unconfirmed: Exact date of the town's moratorium vote (snippets say May 13; the WBNG story read is dated May 15 and gives no date) so the report says 'in May 2026'. Whether the City of Oneonta actually adopted its moratorium was not confirmed. The governor's statewide data center moratorium page returned a JS challenge and was not used; Hoodline results were excluded. Current status of Eco-Yotta's application was not confirmed.

paragraphs: WF Industrial, also known as Wildflower, wants to turn a site with three vacant warehouses in Yaphank, in the Town of Brookhaven, into a $1 billion, 549,000-square-foot data center. The 71-acre site is near the Long Island Expressway's north service road, about 1,000 feet from homes. The plan is on hold: Brookhaven's 18-month moratorium on new data centers, passed unanimously on July 16, 2026, runs to January 2028, and the state's one-year pause on large data centers also applies.

The data center could draw up to 176.6 megawatts of power from the Long Island Power Authority grid, a load LIPA called manageable. Wildflower says its closed-loop cooling needs a one-time fill of about 700,000 gallons of water, "about an Olympic-sized swimming pool." Residents worry about the grid and the aquifer that supplies Long Island's drinking water. "My biggest thing is that it doesn't belong here," said Brookhaven resident Lynne Maher. "There's a robust review process that looks at environmental impacts of the projects, aside from a moratorium," said Michael Bowden, Wildflower's director of development.

The Brookhaven hearings ran nearly six hours. Supervisor Dan Panico turned down calls for a permanent ban, saying any ban would have to come out of the 18-month code-writing process. Next door, the Town of Islip approved its own 18-month moratorium on July 14, 2026; Supervisor Angie Carpenter voted against it, saying it "doesn't really comply with town code or New York State code."

Hubbard Township has tried to get ahead of data centers before one arrives. On Feb. 10, 2026, trustees voted 2-1 to place a one-year moratorium on data centers entering the township, with Trustee Monica Baker abstaining without giving a reason, the Tribune Chronicle reported. Trustee Jason Tedrow said the zoning commission had wanted to ban the facilities outright but learned through the county planning commission that the township could not, so the township's attorney drafted a moratorium instead. "This will give us a 12-month window to allow our zoning commission to hopefully engage the public," Tedrow said.

By July 2026 a Massachusetts real estate developer had approached Hubbard Township trustees about a heavy-industrial property originally intended to be a landfill. Trustees said the project would be 100 to 300 megawatts of power and a $2 billion investment on 75 acres, and Tedrow said the developer would be willing to give the township between $10 million and $30 million. Tedrow called data centers a "net negative" and said the choice would be up to residents. Trustee Eric Lamb said draft zoning would cap noise at 42 decibels at property lines and limit building height to 25 feet.

Residents at the July meeting pushed back. "I will speak for myself and say that I would much rather pay higher taxes than open that door," said Melissa Wade, who also raised the closed Deer Creek Golf Course as a possible site; Tedrow has said that property is a city matter, not a township one. "But data centers, you let one in, and they all come," said resident Melanie Bolovich.

The county's largest data center project is in Lordstown, where SoftBank is working with OpenAI under the Stargate banner. When OpenAI announced five more U.S. Stargate sites in September 2025, it said SoftBank had broken ground in Lordstown on what it called "an advanced data center design which is on track to be operational next year," and that the Lordstown site and a second in Milam County, Texas, could scale to 1.5 gigawatts of power over 18 months.

Trumbull County also led the Mahoning Valley in signatures for Conserve Ohio's proposed constitutional amendment banning data centers over 25 megawatts, with 1,087 of the 7,388 sought as of June 2026. The campaign fell short of the statewide requirement for the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot and now aims for 2027.

Prineville, the seat of Crook County, has hosted large Meta and Apple data center campuses for about 15 years. Meta began building in 2010, and by July 2026 the campus, the company's largest in the country, covered 11 buildings and 4.6 million square feet, with about $2 billion invested. Apple has released much less about its Prineville campus and did not answer local reporters' questions. A city analysis this year put data center employment at about 700 people, most of the jobs added in Prineville since 2008.

Both companies came under property tax exemptions through Oregon's Long-Term Rural Enterprise Zone program, and neither has paid local property taxes so far; the Crook County Assessor's Office put this year's exempted value for data centers at more than $130 million. The 15-year exemptions start expiring next year, and City Manager Steve Forrester says Prineville will roughly double its property tax revenue once they do. Fees that power utilities pay for street access have grown from about $430,000 in 2011 to nearly $11 million. "We are more financially stable now than we have ever been because of the revenue generated by the data center," said longtime councilor Steve Uffelman, filling in as mayor after Jason Beebe resigned in June 2026.

Water is the bigger local worry. Prineville's underground water storage system, funded by Meta and Apple, holds about a year's supply, but state regulators have been limiting new municipal water in the Deschutes Basin as aquifer levels decline. Researchers told a state advisory committee that Meta's Prineville campus used about 70 million gallons of water in 2024, roughly what 420 Prineville households used in 2021. "Everybody I've talked to, they don't want more data centers," said Julie Thompson, a candidate for Crook County commission. Prineville leaders say they probably will not negotiate a full property tax break for the next data center that comes; the governor's Data Center Advisory Committee is due to recommend statewide rules in October 2026.

Energy Capital Partners announced in July 2025 that it would build a $5 billion AI data center at Calpine's York 2 Energy Center in Peach Bottom Township, next to the existing gas plant, but no formal plan has been filed with the township. Because the site is already zoned industrial, Peach Bottom has been writing its own data center ordinance in advance, covering noise, water testing, emergency response and training for local firefighters, who currently lack the equipment to respond to a data center incident.

Residents have pressed officials at repeated workshops. "Nobody has come to us and said, 'Hey, this is what we're planning on doing,'" Planning Commission Chairman Wes Carter said. "Nobody's put forward a land development plan or anything like that." The planning commission has sent its draft ordinance to municipal and county officials for review, ahead of a public comment period and a final vote; no date for that vote has been set.

In Fairview Township, supervisors approved a zoning change in June 2025 allowing data centers as a conditional use with a required sound study and setbacks. The applicant, Fairview Crossroads LLC, wants to build a 750,000-square-foot facility its representative valued at $500 million, adding more than $6 million a year in township tax revenue. Farther north, a developer has approached landowners in East Manchester Township, and rumors of other projects have circulated in Manchester and Windsor townships.

The city of Denton is the center of data center activity in Denton County, and in 2026 it became one of several North Texas cities moving to slow new projects. Denton already hosts two data centers approved by the council in 2024 and 2026: Core Scientific's AI data center, which KERA and the Denton Record-Chronicle reported in August 2026 was nearing full buildout for up to 391 megawatts and leases its capacity to CoreWeave, and a smaller modular facility from QumulusAI, granted a permit on January 13, 2026 and contracted for up to 20 megawatts. Elsewhere in the county, CyrusOne runs smaller operating sites in Carrollton and Lewisville, T5 Data Centers has a site in Fort Worth, and Citigroup operates the Cornerstone Southwest data center in Roanoke.

On August 4, 2026, a 4-3 Denton council majority directed staff to pursue both a temporary moratorium on new data centers and permanent changes to the city's development code. Under a 2025 state law, the city must hold two public hearings and win a supermajority vote to impose such a pause; the moratorium would run 90 days, extendable to 180. Denton Municipal Electric's general manager, Antonio Puente, said the city's transmission system is already near capacity and that anything above 75 megawatts "is likely beyond the capacity that we have today." At the first hearing in September, all 20 speakers supported a moratorium, some wanting it longer or a ban.

A second hearing is set for October 27, 2026, with final consideration expected in early December. "What do these data centers bring to our community? If the only answer is money, then essentially they are giving us nothing in exchange for our resources," resident Seth Fuller said.

Kansas-based Diode Ventures withdrew its proposal for a data center in Henderson County in July 2026, months after residents around Cedar Creek Lake organized against it. The site sat west of the lake between Trinidad and Tool, according to West Cedar Creek Municipal Utility District records obtained by the Fort Worth Report. Cedar Creek Reservoir is owned by the Tarrant Regional Water District and is one of two East Texas lakes that supply most of the raw water for Fort Worth, Arlington and other North Texas cities.

Water was the core of the dispute. In December 2025 emails with the utility district, a Diode project development manager said the project would need between 1 million and 5 million gallons of water per day, the Fort Worth Report found. A Diode spokesperson said that projection did not mean that much would ultimately be used. Records showed the rural utility projected pumping just under 1.5 million gallons a day in 2025 for about 22,400 customers. On May 21, 2026, the utility district approved a temporary suspension of "high-intensity water service commitments" that runs through April 1, 2027. The Tarrant Regional Water District said Diode's application for raw water was incomplete.

In May 2026 more than 200 people packed a Henderson County Commissioners Court meeting in Athens, KLTV reported, and about thirty spoke, all against the data center. "It's a water issue. it's a property value issue. it is a local control issue," said Ashley Cook of Trinidad. Commissioners then adopted a resolution opposing open-loop evaporative cooling in water-constrained regions and calling for enforceable safeguards on grid reliability and ratepayer costs. "This is not a vote approving or denying any specific project today," Pct. 1 Commissioner Wendy Spivey said. Texas counties have no zoning authority. "There's not much the county can do," Spivey later told The Texas Tribune. "We don't have zoning rules and regulations."

Diode told the Tribune it had "determined not to advance the site beyond preliminary planning." Gov. Greg Abbott said in a statement, "Data centers that want to do business in Texas must meet a clear standard. This project did not." The volunteer coalition Save Cedar Creek Lake had gathered thousands of petition signatures. Spivey called the withdrawal "a big, big step in a positive direction" but warned that the landowners are still looking for ways to sell or use the land and that another data center developer could come in.
/data-centers/united-states/texas/hender.unconfirmed: The site's 150 MW figure appears only in a search snippet attributing an 80-150 MW estimate to an opposition group; not read in raw text, so not used. Diode's parent company (Black & Veatch) appeared only in a snippet and is not used.

paragraphs: Two very large projects have been proposed outside Fort Stockton in Pecos County, both built around Permian Basin natural gas rather than the state grid. The bigger is GW Ranch, an off-grid gas power and data center complex on an 8,000-acre site developed by California-based Pacifico Energy. In January 2026 the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality issued what Inside Climate News called the largest air pollution permit in the country for it, authorizing more than 12,000 tons a year of regulated air pollutants and up to 33 million tons a year of greenhouse gases. Engineering News-Record reported the permits cover 35 gas turbines able to generate up to 7.65 gigawatts, plus up to 750 megawatts of solar and 1.8 gigawatts of battery storage.

In August 2026 Amazon confirmed it had acquired GW Ranch, filing for three buildings, together called the Pecos County Data Center, at 6000 TX-18, about 11 miles north of Fort Stockton, each at 189,060 square feet and $300 million, with construction scheduled from August to December 2026. Pacifico had earlier put the project's needed investment at about $12 billion. On water, an Amazon spokesperson told ENR: "The initial phase requires no water for power-generation cooling, and later phases are designed to rely primarily on brackish groundwater, which does not compete with the community drinking water supply." Research cited by ENR estimated the plants could eventually burn 1 to 2 billion cubic feet of gas a day, 4 to 7 percent of 2025 Permian Basin gas production.

The second project, Project Horizon, was announced in October 2025 by AI startup Poolside as a 2-gigawatt campus on the Mitchell family's Longfellow Ranch, with CoreWeave as anchor tenant for a first 250-megawatt phase. By August 2026 CoreWeave had dropped out; on August 17 Poolside described its flagship project as "a 400 MW data center in unincorporated Pecos County, Texas." The county had already created a tax reinvestment zone for the site in January 2025 and considered an abatement agreement with CoreWeave in January 2026.

Because GW Ranch starts off the grid, it is unclear how a statewide pause on new data center grid connections, announced August 3, 2026 by Gov. Greg Abbott, would affect it. Amazon says the system is designed to move to grid-connected service later.

Shackelford County's largest town, Albany, is about 35 miles northeast of Abilene, and the county is now home to one of the largest AI data center campuses under construction in the US. Vantage Data Centers' "Frontier" campus sits on about 1,200 acres at Highway 604 and Highway 351, west of Albany, and is being built for OpenAI and Oracle's Stargate project. At full build-out it is planned to hold 10 buildings totaling 1,400 megawatts of power. Vantage broke ground in December 2025; the first building is due to go live in the second half of 2026.

Commissioners approved the project unanimously in July 2025, creating a reinvestment zone and a 10-year tax abatement under which Vantage will pay the county $10 million a year instead of property taxes -- a sum the Albany News said could raise the county's operating budget by nearly 200 percent. Vantage also pledged $150,000 a year to local charities and up to 10 college scholarships a year, and says the campus will bring 250 full-time jobs and up to 6,500 workers at peak construction. Because the site falls in the Clyde school district, Albany's schools get no direct benefit. Construction traffic has been the most visible effect: gravel trucks are expected to peak through early 2027, and resident Twylia Waldon told commissioners trucks pass "one after the other" and "do not follow the speed limits."

In July 2026, Bolt Data and Energy proposed a second project, Project North, on the Buck Nail Ranch about 16 miles west of Albany. Bolt representative Peter Richards said the company would "co-locate power and compute together" and expects to put excess power back onto the grid. As of August 2026, Bolt had not confirmed the project's size, water use, jobs or timeline. Commissioners have accepted Bolt's tax abatement application and formed a citizen advisory committee, but had not approved the project. "I don't see how specifically Albany and Shackleford County, the people who live here, grew up here, are benefiting from these data centers," resident James Scottie said.

Culpeper County, southwest of Loudoun County, has approved a string of data center campuses in a few years, most in a county-designated Technology Zone beside the town of Culpeper. The county told WJLA in July 2026 that two data centers were operating, with several more approved or under construction, plus an Amazon campus outside the zone. Growth on that scale has brought organized opposition, a lawsuit, and now a fight over the transmission lines and substation needed to power the industry.

Amazon, through its Marvell Developments subsidiary, rezoned 243 acres on Germanna Highway in Stevensburg, a former horse farm, for a two-building campus of up to 430,000 square feet. Supervisors approved it 4-3 in April 2022 despite the planning commission's recommendation to deny it, and neighboring landowners sued, arguing the vote was illegal spot zoning. "Now it will be like living in a Wal-Mart parking lot," resident Ralph Pritt said at the time. DCD reported AWS planned to invest about $500 million; the project is now under construction.

In the Technology Zone, supervisors rezoned 121 acres on Nalles Mill Road in December 2023 for Cielo Digital Infrastructure's three buildings, two of 96 megawatts and one of 48; EdgeCore later bought the project, now under construction as EdgeCore Culpeper. In July 2024 they rezoned 69 acres on Nalles Mill and Keyser roads, 4-3, for Red Ace Capital Management's two four-story buildings; Supervisor Susan Gugino said it would be the last such project she'd approve because the zone was full. A 426-acre proposal still filed under the placeholder name XX Tech Park, developer unnamed, seeks 900 megawatts and has been pending since 2024.

Not every proposal has gone through. Two data center bids in Brandy Station, near Culpeper Battlefields State Park, drew resistance; after the planning commission recommended denial, the applicant withdrew. Town residents formed the Coalition to Save Culpeper, and member Andrew Dowdy told the Virginia Mercury that officials had largely ignored residents' concerns.

Power is now the central fight. Dominion Energy and its Valley Link partners have proposed a 115-mile high-voltage line ending at a substation on 88 acres of forest in Richardsville. At a May 19, 2026 meeting, most supervisors made clear the county did not want the substation, and a Dominion representative said, "We do not have an alternative." Dominion says it will file with the State Corporation Commission this fall regardless of the county's position. The county cites a study projecting $2.2 billion in data center tax revenue over 15 years, but unlike Loudoun and Prince William counties, it has no special tax on data center computer equipment.

Wise County's existing data center is Mineral Gap, a 65,000-square-foot facility built by DP Facilities on 22 acres of the county's Lonesome Pine Business and Technology Park. It opened in April 2017 as a $65 million project aimed at federal and state government agencies as well as commercial clients, backed by a $350,000 grant from the Virginia Tobacco Commission; a 3.5-megawatt solar farm on a former coal mine helps power it.

A much larger project is now proposed for the same park. In February 2026 Cardinal News reported plans for the Wise Innovation Hub, about 2 million square feet of data center space in nine buildings, built in phases over roughly 10 years and powered by an on-site natural gas plant. Red Post Energy, a Houston-based power producer, signed a letter of intent in December 2025 to design the generation. CEO Lance Medlin said the first 100 megawatts or so could come online in about three years and eventually scale to 500 or 600 megawatts, with 20% to 30% of the output going back to the grid. Brian Falin, the county's industrial development director, said he did not expect heavy water use and that taxes from each building could bring $3 million to $5 million a year: "We're not going to rush this," he said.

The gas plan, nicknamed the "Maverick Project," has drawn criticism. Appalachian Voices wrote in March 2026 that residents who had repeatedly asked the board of supervisors for more transparency learned about it from a LinkedIn post instead, and that the developers have indicated a desire to partner with the gas pipeline company Enbridge on the project's power supply.

China Mobile, the state-owned Chinese carrier, builds its largest data centers at home. The biggest sits in the Horinger New Area outside Hohhot, Inner Mongolia: Yicai reported in April 2024 that it had gone into operation with 6.7 EFLOPS of computing power and about 20,000 AI accelerator cards, 85 percent of them made in China. A company planning executive told Yicai that China Mobile had 12 such computing hubs running, with more planned in Harbin and Guiyang. Light Reading reported in July 2024 that China Mobile had placed a 19.1 billion yuan ($2.6 billion) order for computing gear with Chinese suppliers, including Huakun Zhenyu, which builds hardware on Huawei's Kunpeng and Ascend processors.

Abroad, the international arm is still growing. In June 2026 the Malaysian developer Tanco signed a non-binding agreement with China Mobile International to consider a 50-megawatt data center in Port Dickson, Negeri Sembilan, DCD reported, with two years to reach a firm deal; DCD noted it was unclear whether Tanco had prior experience building or running a data center.

In the United States, where China Mobile still runs network hubs at data centers despite a 2019 denial of its carrier license, a bipartisan House committee investigation reported in August 2026 that it found at least 143 active China Mobile network assets in American facilities. The Federal Communications Commission voted on April 30, 2026 to advance rules that could bar China Mobile from operating US data centers altogether; China's Ministry of Commerce urged the US to "stop its wrong practices immediately."

Hut 8, a Miami-based company that made its name in bitcoin mining, is now developing three AI data center campuses in the US. The furthest along is River Bend in West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, about 30 miles north of Baton Rouge: a 15-year, $7.0 billion lease covering 245 megawatts of IT capacity, with Fluidstack as tenant and Google backstopping the lease payments. Entergy Louisiana has secured an initial 330 megawatts of utility capacity, and the first data hall is due in the second quarter of 2027. Parish President Kenny Havard called it "a generational opportunity."

In Nueces County, Texas, Hut 8 is building Beacon Point, a 525-acre campus near Robstown. An unnamed "high-investment-grade tenant" signed a 352MW lease there in May 2026 and a second lease in July 2026 that doubled its contracted IT capacity to 704 MW, on a 1GW interconnection agreement. Hut 8's Hailey Miller said cooling water for the closed-loop system would be trucked in from outside the county: "Under no circumstance will we use municipal water for cooling."

Illinois is where Hut 8 has been fought. It proposed the 500-megawatt Logan Prairie Data Center on farmland in Laenna Township, near Latham in Logan County; the county board passed a 12-month moratorium 6-4 in May 2026, which the state's attorney later called not legally binding because it skipped the Zoning Board of Appeals.

Hut 8 then offered Latham, a village of 350 people, $8 million to $11 million a year for 15 years to annex and rezone the site. Village President Theodore Allen, who once opposed the project, backed the deal, but by late July told Illinois Times the plan would fail if put to a vote. The August 3 village meeting was cancelled, and the county's August hearings were also called off after the state's attorney found technical mistakes in Hut 8's applications.

South Korea's data center fight is in and around Seoul, where most of the country's data centers are. On August 12, 2026, the heads of all 25 Seoul districts agreed to ask the city for tougher limits on new data centers and to seek a change to the Building Act so districts could refuse permits in semi-residential, semi-industrial and commercial areas. Because data centers count as telecommunications facilities, local governments have few grounds to restrict them across about 88% of Seoul.

Seventeen of 33 data center projects pursued in the capital region in 2024 and 2025 were delayed or scrapped, the Korea Herald reported. In Geumcheon-gu, disputes between residents and developers have turned into criminal complaints. "Residents are increasingly concerned about data centers being built in densely populated residential areas," said Cho Yu-jin, mayor of Yeongdeungpo-gu.

In Incheon's Dohwa-dong, KDB Infrastructure Asset Management plans a data center with 80 megawatts of power on about 58,000 square meters, permitted by Michuhol-gu in April 2023. Residents object that apartments sit about 150 meters away and a school about 300 meters; three shaved their heads at a May rally, and more than 6,400 signed against it. The newly elected district mayor, Kim Jung-sik, opposes the project, and in July the district formed a 19-member council of residents, officials and builders, which was to hold its first meeting in August.

Outside the capital, the national government wants 18.4 gigawatts of AI data center capacity by 2035. The "Stargate Korea" plan announced with OpenAI in October 2025, one site with SK in South Jeolla and one with Samsung in Pohang, had little to show nearly a year later: Samsung SDS said "nothing has been confirmed," and an industry source said the companies were still looking for sites with enough power and water.

Ascension Parish began writing data center rules in August 2026 before anyone had publicly asked to build one. At its August 6 meeting at the courthouse in Donaldsonville, after several people spoke against data centers, the parish council approved a resolution asking the Planning and Zoning Commission to draft guidelines for what it calls "high impact development facilities", the Gonzales Weekly Citizen reported. "For the record, we do not know of a data center who wants to build anywhere in the parish," said council chair Chase Melancon. "If they were to apply for a data center in the parish right now, we have nothing as far as setbacks, noise. We don't have anything to hold them to." He said training sessions with officials from places that host the facilities "showed us that we're not ready to even have the conversation." Council member Joel Robert suggested a moratorium until the rules were finished.

In September the zoning commission recommended amendments requiring any data center applicant to hold two public meetings before applying to rezone land, requiring the operator to independently generate, operate and maintain its own power, and lowering the allowed noise level from 50 to 45 decibels, WBRZ reported. The council introduced the code amendment at its September 17 meeting in Gonzales. "Right now, families in the parish learn about industrial projects only after the decisions are already made behind closed doors," resident Barbara Bourgeois said, asking for transparency. "At least 11 of our own elected and appointed officials have signed NDAs."

The first named project arrived in the middle of that process. On August 31, ONE Nuclear, a Florida-based developer, announced a binding letter of intent with an unnamed "prominent Louisiana landowner group" for site control of Project Cayman: a 2.88-gigawatt gas-fired power plant and a 700MW, 2.88GWh battery system alongside a data center campus, near the 17,000-acre RiverPlex MegaPark on the west bank of the Mississippi, POWER magazine reported. The company did not disclose who would build or use the data center. Despite its name, the project is gas; ONE Nuclear says its strategy is to build gas plants for industrial sites that could later move to small modular reactors. It said it would hold public information meetings with parishes and agencies through the end of 2026. The company's merger with Hennessy Capital Investment Corp. VII, already approved by Hennessy's shareholders, was expected to close by year-end. On the same west bank, Hyundai has begun pre-construction work on a $5.8 billion steel mill in the Modeste area.
/data-centers/united-states/louisiana/as.unconfirmed: Business Report's story on Entergy's $498 million investment for two unnamed RiverPlex users returned only its teaser (1,218 chars); the figure is not stated. Hoodline's Project Cayman story is an aggregator and not used. mgrid.org read but not used (analysis site with no original reporting); WBRZ's 'HUT 8 $12 billion' figure for West Feliciana conflicts with other reporting and is not repeated. Whether the council gave the code final approval after the September 17 introduction was not found. Zoning commissioner Petite's first name was not given.

paragraphs: Webster County has no planning and zoning. Voters turned it down in 2005 and 2007, Presiding Commissioner Paul Ipock told the Springfield Business Journal. That is why a data center could go up on Rifle Range Road, just north of Marshfield, before most residents knew it existed. Ipock said commissioners first learned of it on April 29, 2026 from a Facebook post. The owner is Lumon Solutions LLC, formed in October 2025, whose partners include Trent Overhue, the Springfield developer who bought Plaza Towers in a 2025 foreclosure sale, and Ashton Owens. The county's May 6 statement, citing the company, described a "small-scale, high-performance computing facility" on a 5-acre site, cooled by a closed-loop system using a few hundred gallons of water a month from a residential-style well. "In short, this particular development does not appear to be one of the massive, resource-consuming hyperscale data centers that have been built elsewhere in the country," the commission said. Overhue said the center would use 10 megawatts and sits next to a Webster Electric Cooperative substation. He declined to name its customer, citing nondisclosure agreements.

About 800 people packed the Marshfield High School auditorium for a special commission meeting on May 11, the Springfield Daily Citizen reported. Residents raised water, groundwater contamination, power, noise and heat, and asked commissioners to sign a one-year moratorium that a lawyer hired by residents had drafted. When a resident asked about a small data center near Omaha that Overhue said he had been a partner in, he declined to give details, citing nondisclosure agreements, and the crowd erupted. Tom Houston, the electric co-op's general manager, said the project would not raise residents' bills; one audience member accused the co-op of soliciting it, which Houston denied. Two days later Lumon posted that it would proceed: "Political pressure does not make a lawful project unlawful. Misinformation does not create legal authority where none exists. Public outrage does not rewrite the rules in the middle of the process."

The commission warned residents that without zoning its "authority to regulate land use and development may be more limited than some of the proposals assume." On June 16 the three commissioners signed a six-month temporary moratorium on new data centers, solar, wind and battery storage systems in the county, the Webster County Citizen reported, citing concerns about grid capacity, round-the-clock noise and drainage. It does not affect the Lumon site, which was already under construction. The newspaper also reported, citing a courthouse source, that anger after the May meeting led to several anonymous threats against commissioners.

Inside Marshfield's city limits, the Board of Aldermen voted on April 23 to require a conditional use permit for data centers in the heavy industrial district, meaning public hearings and an aldermen vote. City Administrator Sam Rost said the change followed inquiries from Swarm Systems, a New York-based company. Its website had advertised a 20-megawatt "Missouri campus" on 8.2 acres at 630 George St. in the city's industrial park, "ready for service in mid-2027". In May the company said it was pausing, the Springfield Business Journal reported. "There was nothing there to stop Lumon Solutions from going ahead and rolling dozers," said Swarm's Amir Atefi. "They didn't ask anyone or tell anyone. It's not a good look for the industry, and it's not the right way to do business."
/data-centers/united-states/missouri/web.unconfirmed: OzarksFirst (KOLR) returned 35 characters and is not used. KY3's May 11 story was fetched but not needed beyond the Daily Citizen's fuller account. The Webster County Citizen dates the big meeting May 13; the Daily Citizen, SBJ and the county's own update all say May 11, which is used. Lumon's claimed $500,000 a year in sales tax and under 5 gallons of water a day are company figures and left out of the page's voice; the county statement's 'few hundred gallons a month' is attributed. Whether the Lumon site is now operating was not found.

paragraphs: After a meeting that ran more than four hours, the Piqua Commission approved a development agreement on November 3, 2025, for a data center in the I-75 Exit 78 Business and Industrial Park at Farrington and Washington Roads, Miami Valley Today reported. It passed as an emergency measure, waiving the usual three readings. City officials said they could not name the company because of a nondisclosure agreement. City Manager Paul Oberdorfer said he did not know who it was. DCD reported the agreement was with J5 LLC, doing business as Shaytura LLC, for two 350,000-square-foot buildings on about 607 acres, built over three to five years. The terms included a 15-year, 100 percent exemption on the buildings' added value, with payments in lieu of taxes to the city and schools, and a 30-year real property tax exemption. Economic Development Director Chris Schmiesing described a $1 billion investment with about 50 full-time jobs.

Water was the first worry. Utilities Director Kevin Krejny said the city's plant, which draws on the Great Miami River, Piqua Quarry and Swift Run Lake, can treat 6.7 million gallons a day. The city uses about 2.2 million, and the project's peak draw would be capped at 2 million on the hottest summer days. By August 2026, Schmiesing was describing a closed-loop system using about as much water as "two full service restaurants".

The second fight was over power. On August 18, 2026, before a standing-room crowd, the commission voted 4-1 for a 30-year franchise letting AES Ohio build and run electric facilities to serve J5 LLC, with a $1 million annual franchise fee paid by the customer, Miami Valley Today reported. Separately, Meta had pledged $8 million to the city (officials have not said whether Meta is behind J5 LLC), which interim city manager Rick Byron linked to first-responder needs such as a $2.5 million ladder truck. Commissioner Paul Simmons cast the only no vote. He had said the week before that 94.5 percent of the people there spoke out against the ordinance, and that residents had been "disenfranchised out of the referendum process last November" by the emergency vote. "I believe in our community and that our best days are in front of us. I support this project," said Vice Mayor Frank DeBrosse. Resident Jonathan Wessel told the commission the franchise was "the last piece of leverage that the city has in this deal." Power director RJ Monnier said the city does not buy power from AES and is "not subsidizing this data center in any way."

The citizen group Save Piqua then began circulating a referendum petition to suspend the franchise ordinance and put it to a public vote, according to a statement from the group published by Miami Valley Today. The group said it had filed petitions on August 11 for a charter amendment banning data centers and cryptocurrency mining in the city, along with recall petitions against Mayor James Vetter, DeBrosse and Commissioner Rick Walker.

Oklahoma's data center story starts in Pryor, where Google's campus at MidAmerica Industrial Park is, by the company's account, its second-largest in the world. The Frontier obtained its water records: from July 2024 to June 2025 it used more than 1.1 billion gallons and discharged about 253 million gallons of wastewater into the Neosho River, with the rest lost to evaporation. In February 2026 The Frontier counted at least 10 new data centers under construction or awaiting approval across the state, and Google alone had announced five new Oklahoma projects in the past few months. Google's planned sites include two campuses in Muskogee County near Summit and Council Hill, a campus in Stillwater and "Project Spring" in Sand Springs. The Oklahoma Water Resources Board expects state water demand to grow 18 percent over 20 years. "The new and emerging users, such as data centers, will contribute to the strain depending on how data centers source water," board engineer Yohanes Sugeng told lawmakers in October 2025.

Pushback has changed some designs. Beale Infrastructure switched its $800 million Project Atlas in Coweta to air cooling after criticism that it would use up to 5.4 million gallons of water a day, The Frontier reported, and said its Project Mustang in Claremore would be air-cooled too. Beale withdrew Project Atlas on March 30, 2026, after weeks of opposition; the land was never rezoned, News On 6 reported. The developers of Project Spring said it would use a dry cooling system, at least in its early phases. News 9 reported that Claremore's council approved Project Mustang on May 18, 2026 after nearly two hours of public comment, and that a conservation group, Land Legacy, sued in March over an easement covering part of the Sand Springs site.

Governor Kevin Stitt signed House Bill 2992, the Data Center Consumer Ratepayer Protection Act of 2026, on May 11. It took effect July 1. It requires new data centers, crypto mines and AI computing facilities adding 75 megawatts or more to sign long-term agreements covering the infrastructure costs they cause, and requires developers to notify the Corporation Commission, county commissioners and neighboring landowners within 60 days of buying land, StateImpact Oklahoma and Data Center Knowledge reported. "This bill makes it clear that when you plug into Oklahoma's world-class energy grid, you come to the table as a partner and do your part to cover the costs," Stitt said. PSO had filed a large load tariff with the commission, and OG&E said Google would cover grid connection costs for the three data centers it agreed to power in Muskogee County and Stillwater. Ari Peskoe of Harvard Law School's Electricity Law Initiative told Data Center Knowledge that such agreements may only partly protect consumers if utilities overbuild for AI demand that never materializes.

Cities have moved on their own. Oklahoma City imposed a moratorium on new data center applications running through December 31, 2026. About a month later, after data center employees crowded the council chambers, the council voted 7-2 to let facilities of up to 75 megawatts apply and to exempt two named sites, including a Scale Datacenters facility serving Cerebras, the Oklahoma City Free Press reported. "Where does that stop?" asked Councilor JoBeth Hamon, who voted no with James Cooper. Pawhuska's Public Works Authority voted 3-2 for a full moratorium through the end of 2026 after a proposal to convert a vacant carpet mill into an AI data center, News 9 reported.

Muskogee County has three large data center projects on the way. In November 2025 Google, Muskogee County, the City of Muskogee and Port Muskogee announced two new Google campuses near Summit and Council Hill, part of the company's two-year, $9 billion Oklahoma investment, KTUL reported. "We are excited to welcome Google to Muskogee County as they begin work on building two data center campuses, which will be transformational for our community," said County Commissioner Kenny Payne. OG&E is to supply the power under contracts in which Google covers the infrastructure costs of serving it. Google also said it would give $1 million to the Muskogee community for schools, small businesses and trades training. The third project is Core Scientific's site at Port Muskogee's industrial park, first announced in 2022 as a crypto mine. DCD reported that Core Scientific and CoreWeave broke ground there on a 100MW AI facility with about 70MW of IT load. Public Radio Tulsa reported that the company now plans to expand it into a 1.5-gigawatt AI campus, which would be the state's largest.

Water is where the county has seen changes on the ground. The City of Muskogee, home to two existing data centers, raised water and other utility rates 2.2 percent, plus a $7.75 monthly sewer increase, to fund a new wastewater treatment plant, The Frontier reported. City spokesperson Judy Villalobos said the increases were related to the planned data centers, although the city could have handled their discharge without a new plant. The Council Hill campus sits within Muskogee Rural Water District #3, which has about 650 members. Vice-chair Howard Whatley said Google expects to need only about 20,000 gallons a day, and that the district's agreement makes Google pay for any upgrades needed to serve it. He said the district has rejected applicants who wanted large withdrawals. "We're not going to take water away from citizens for a project like that," Whatley said. "That wouldn't be neighborly."

Open opposition has been small but has started. In August 2026 more than 50 people came to the city's first data center town hall, organized by residents with Native advocacy groups including Honor the Earth, Public Radio Tulsa reported. "We're not getting clear answers," said Honor the Earth volunteer coordinator Patricia Kaseca, a Muscogee (Creek) Nation citizen, who said she had waited three weeks on a records request. Villalobos said only one open records request was outstanding, held up by a required legal review, and that officials are always willing to talk to residents at city hall.

A search snippet from it described months of Muscogee (Creek) Nation town halls against a proposed AI data center; that could not be read and is not stated. DCD's placement of Muskogee in 'West Oklahoma' is wrong and not repeated. Port Muskogee's $4 billion investment figure is a port claim and left out. Core Scientific's press release was not used.

paragraphs: Claremore's city council approved a data center of at least $1 billion in May 2026, and within weeks residents had filed recall petitions against all nine councilors. The project is Project Mustang, a Beale Infrastructure campus on about 290 acres of the Claremore Industrial Park, three miles north of downtown Claremore along Route 66, on land zoned industrial for decades, the Tulsa World reported. The terms were set in a tax increment plan a review committee of Rogers County taxing entities recommended on March 31, 2026. Under it, three incentive districts would be created on 255 acres, one for each data center. Within them Beale and its end user would pay no property tax for 25 years each, making payments in lieu of taxes of $4.75 per square foot instead, plus a $250,000 annual "community betterment payment" to the city. Jeff Sabin, the lawyer who drafted the plan for the city, told the committee a Claremore data center would not be economically viable for Beale without the incentives. "It's a massive amount of investment, but very few jobs," he said. The plan called for 35 permanent jobs per phase.

At the March committee meeting, opponents held up signs reading "Let the people vote." "They're not going to be able to see the stars at night," said Teresa Luce, who had visited neighbors whose land abuts the site. "They're gonna have to listen to that hum all night long, whatever that might be." After a packed public hearing on May 4, the City Council approved the project on May 18. City Hall was at standing-room capacity and people rotated in from outside to meet fire code, News On 6 reported. "How are you going to compensate me and my neighbors? We get no benefit from you at all," resident Debbie Cassita told the council. Beale said the air-cooled buildings would use about 20,000 gallons of water a day. Its public policy chief, Tony Burkart, described a "community-first" approach.

The Tulsa World later reported that the land deal and main agreements were final, with Beale bound to invest at least $1 billion over roughly five to seven years. The city said Beale had put up a $21.552 million irrevocable letter of credit as security and would pay $5 million into a Community Betterment Fund. "I know we've done this the right way, and we've done the right thing by our community for the long run," City Manager John Feary said. Residents filed recall petitions against all nine city councilors and three referendum petitions against the project's approving ordinances in early June, the Claremore Daily Progress reported. The city later found all three referendum petitions invalid because copies were not filed with the city clerk before signatures were gathered, as state law requires.

Google built its first data center in The Dalles in 2006, and it now takes about a third of the city's water, OPB reported in January 2026, up from 12 percent in 2012. The company completed another building in 2025 and planned one more in 2026. In 2021 the city signed two agreements with Google. One guaranteed the company a set amount of water each year to cool two new buildings. Under the other, Google transferred about $28.5 million in water infrastructure to the city. Google had previously argued that its water use was a trade secret, until The Oregonian/OregonLive sued for the records and the city settled. Google's Ben Townsend told OPB the company had been protecting the "physical security of assets that are critical to operations."

The Dalles is now asking Congress for 150 acres of the Mount Hood National Forest around its reservoir, so it can raise the dam and roughly triple storage to about 3,000 acre-feet without Forest Service environmental review. The project is expected to cost about $70 million. Rep. Cliff Bentz's bill has passed the House. "Google is really not a factor in this at all," Mayor Richard Mays said. OPB found, however, that the city's 2024 water master plan projects at least a million gallons a day for an unnamed industrial user, the same amount Google uses. The plan also forecasts residential water rates climbing 99 percent by 2036. "Obviously, the great driver of demand for water in The Dalles is Google," said John DeVoe of WaterWatch of Oregon. Environmental groups warn that more diversion from the Dog River, where threatened salmon and steelhead run, would warm the river. Mays and the city's retired public works director called OPB's story inaccurate. OPB published a line-by-line review, corrected one figure and stood by the reporting.

The money flows the other way through tax deals. OPB reported that Google's property taxes are discounted by 92 percent under its agreements with the city and Wasco County, and that it paid $7.3 million in 2025 including a community service fee. For 2025-26, one of Google's newest data centers generated $1.56 million in property taxes, a $2.5 million community service fee, a $5.76 million guaranteed annual payment and a one-time $3 million initial payment, according to the county assessor's report described by Columbia Community Connection. In August 2026 county commissioners took up an ordinance to put up to $15 million of those one-time revenues into an endowment that could not be spent until July 1, 2041. "These abatement programs are a one-time incentive designed to attract investment to the community, and the revenue received through them represents a one-time opportunity," Assessor Jill Amery wrote.
/data-centers/united-states/oregon/wasco.unconfirmed: The Sierra Club piece returned nothing (212-byte page). KLCC's June 2026 segment on data center costs was fetched but not used. The DCD figures for Google's 2024 withdrawal (461.1 million gallons) appeared only in a search snippet and are not stated. A search snippet quoted Mays in March 2026 saying a position 'is coming back to haunt us today'; no source was read for it, so it is dropped. Whether the endowment ordinance passed was not found.

paragraphs: Aiken County has recruited data centers instead of fighting them. The largest is Meta's $800 million campus in the Sage Mill Industrial Park in Graniteville, expected to open in spring 2027. Aiken Electric will supply the power, backed by a solar field in Orangeburg County that will offset "some of the use that Meta will have, not all of it," said Will Williams of the Western SC Economic Development Partnership.

The County Council has since approved incentives for two smaller multi-tenant projects for customers it would not name: a DC BLOX data center near North Augusta, approved 8-1 in January 2025 over the objection of council member Mike Kellems, and a $32 million, 60,000-square-foot building beside Sage Mill for Clop Aiken SC LLC, an Oppidan Investment Co. subsidiary, approved that June. "We've offered multiple [fee in lieu of property taxes agreements] to solar farms that never happened," council chairman Gary Bunker said, cautioning that incentives do not guarantee a project.

The federal government is planning the biggest project yet. In July 2026 the National Nuclear Security Administration picked the engineering firm Amentum to negotiate a lease for a 1-gigawatt AI data center at the Savannah River Site, backed by its own gas power and, later, nuclear power. The Department of Energy says the pick "does not constitute a final lease award" and still needs permitting and security review.

The first pushback has come from horse country. At a packed County Council meeting, residents raised rumors of a data center and gas plant off New Holland Road that officials said they had not discussed. "District 1 has a large community of horse people," said council member Ron Felder, who said residents had been offered "significant amounts of money for their property."

Coryell County has no data center under construction, but two things are worth watching. The first is Fort Hood, which straddles Coryell and Bell counties: in January 2026 the Army solicited bids for commercial data centers on leased land there and at three other posts, and in March conditionally selected developers for two of them, Fort Bliss and Dugway Proving Ground. Fort Hood has had no award yet. Federal contracting documents describe parcels under consideration there, including one within a quarter mile of homes and businesses, and ask bidders to describe outreach to "assess local sentiment and any risks or opposition."

The second is the wave of data center projects elsewhere in Central Texas, which has split county commissioners over how to respond. Commissioner Scott Weddle has pushed a resolution, modeled on one Johnson County passed, urging the Legislature to tighten the reporting and safeguard requirements set by the 2025 state law known as Senate Bill 6. County Judge Roger Miller wants concrete data on local impacts before acting, and has raised concern that new restrictions could limit landowners' right to sell or lease their property. Commissioners have discussed the resolution as a working document without yet adopting it.

Midland County's leaders have said they will take data centers on one condition: that the companies bring their own power and water. "I believe the only appropriate way for data centers to be developed in West Texas is for them to solve their own water solutions and their own power solutions, and that it be out away from neighborhoods and families," Mayor Lori Blong said on KWEL radio on May 13, 2026, the Permian Press reported. She said the city should not sell them municipal water: "We've just spent most of this show talking about our water limitations, but we also have energy limitations." County Judge Terry Johnson said the day before that three data center groups had approached the county, all describing closed-loop cooling and on-site natural gas generation. "These folks want to be good neighbors, so they're always trying to improve what they're doing," he said.

In September 2025, FO Permian Partners and HiVolt Energy, both headquartered in Midland, said they had 320 acres under option with a landowner about 30 minutes southeast of downtown, part of a 3,200-acre tract, the Midland Reporter-Telegram reported. The first phase promises 150 megawatts of behind-the-meter gas power, about what the whole city of Midland uses in its lowest-demand winter hours, from reciprocating engines with battery backup, off the grid; the developers claim access to more than 5 gigawatts of gas supply. No data center builder had signed on. Co-founder Davis Farish said the partners "still have a steep hill to climb to attract a premier data center builder to West Texas." HiVolt's Andy Deck said local ownership mattered: "A lot of times, big projects like this, people take a lot of value out of the Permian Basin. We liked the ability to keep value in the Permian Basin."

The broader Permian question is power. At a Texas Senate committee hearing on May 11, Blong said she was "very frustrated with the lack of gas-fired power generation in West Texas." The Public Utility Commission is collecting water-use data from data centers and crypto mines statewide and must report by the end of 2026, ahead of the 2027 legislative session, the Permian Press reported.

Mitchell County's data center is Barber Lake, a 300-megawatt AI computing campus at 951 County Road 204, north of Interstate 20 and just outside Colorado City, built by Cipher Digital (formerly Cipher Mining) on a site that has grown from 250 acres to nearly 600, San Angelo LIVE! reported. Fluidstack leases the whole site. In its first deal in September 2025, Cipher agreed to deliver 168MW of IT load under a $3 billion, 10-year lease, with Google backstopping $1.4 billion of Fluidstack's obligations and taking a 5.4 percent stake in Cipher, DCD reported. A third deal took Fluidstack to the full 300MW. Anthropic is the AI user, with Google TPUs running its models. San Angelo LIVE! reported the first phase was due to deliver capacity in September 2026, with rent starting in October and a second phase targeted for January 2027.

Colorado City's own water system failed in July 2026, when thunderstorms knocked out power and backup generators at a well-pump station and taps ran dry, on top of years of aging pipes. Cipher, Fluidstack and Anthropic presented a $10 million check on September 14 to open the Colorado City Water Infrastructure Foundation, a nonprofit to fund repairs. Mayor Ruben Hurt said the money is part of a $27 million package with a $10 million USDA grant and a separate $7 million grant. The city's list includes a new well field, a new water tower, replacement of a 16-inch main running about two miles through town and a second line to the school district. Cipher says Barber Lake uses only on-site non-potable water and does not connect to the city system, and Hurt has said the data center is not a city water customer. "We could see that Colorado City was a community with deep roots," Cipher CEO Tyler Page said.

Lee Roy Miller, the Republican nominee for the county's Precinct 2 commissioner seat, is a cattleman who told San Angelo LIVE! he runs less than half the cattle he did 20 years ago because he is still uneasy about water after the 2011 drought. He called the data center a necessary economic development project and said he was glad the city was getting help with its water system.
/data-centers/united-states/texas/mitche.unconfirmed: NewsWest 9's story on Colorado City's water outages returned an access-denied page, and KTAB's (BigCountryHomepage) returned a 35-character shell; neither is used. A search snippet said families recently went four days without running water; no readable source carried it, so it is dropped. Hoodline's version is an aggregator and not used. The claim that Barber Lake draws no city water is the companies' and the mayor's, attributed as such. Whether Barber Lake actually began delivering capacity in September 2026 was not confirmed.

paragraphs: The biggest data center story in Potter County is being built outside it. Fermi America's Project Matador, the "President Donald J. Trump Advanced Energy and Intelligence Campus" co-founded by former Governor and Energy Secretary Rick Perry, sits next to the Pantex Plant about 35 miles north of Amarillo in Carson County, on land leased from the Texas Tech University System. But Amarillo, the Potter County seat, is selling it water. On October 14, 2025 the City Council voted 5-0 for a water supply agreement, KVII reported. According to the Amarillo Tribune, the agreement provides 2.5 million gallons a day from the municipal supply for 20 years, with two 10-year renewals, at twice the rate a commercial user inside the city pays. Fermi is to cover the cost of the improvements, including two new wells in Carson County. Fermi's IPO filing said it expects to need up to 5.5 million gallons a day, and the Tribune reported the city and Fermi both expected the company to return seeking that amount. The agreement does not say what happens if Fermi exceeds its allotment.

Part of Amarillo's supply comes from the Ogallala Aquifer, which is being drained faster than it recharges and also supplies the region's farmers and ranchers, The Texas Tribune reported. Residents protested the deal in front of the Potter County courthouse in late September 2025. "Wealth here is the water," said Will Masters of the nonprofit Ogallala Life. "If the water is not here, this area is impoverished." Mayor Cole Stanley said the city would charge Fermi more than regular customers and make it build its own infrastructure. "Then we'll be the beneficiary of the additional jobs that pay well, new residents who build homes and put in additional businesses," he said. He added that Fermi "is going to need to step up and hold their own forums and engage with those citizens directly." The Amarillo Tribune reported that the first gigawatt of gas generation at the campus would use roughly 1.5 billion to 2 billion gallons of water in its first year.

Potter County government has its own, much smaller, deal. In January 2026 commissioners approved leasing a parking lot near the Santa Fe Building downtown to Duos Edge for an edge data center, at $18,000 a year for five years with an option to extend, KVII reported.
/data-centers/united-states/texas/potter.unconfirmed: Two MyHighPlains (KAMR) stories, on Mayor Stanley's explanation of the deal and on Fermi's response to water concerns, returned 35-character bot-wall shells and are not used. Citizen Portal's account of students asking the council to end the partnership is an aggregator and not used; the underlying KVII meeting coverage could not be found under the 2026 date. The 'first gigawatt' water figure is Fermi's own projection, attributed. The site's own record puts Project Matador in Amarillo 79068; every source places it in Carson County. Whether Fermi has returned to seek 5.5 million gallons a day was not found.

paragraphs: Vulcan Core wanted to put a 12-megawatt Bitcoin mining facility in a small building near downtown Tyler, at 1101 and 1105 West Erwin Street, in an existing building on about 1.8 acres zoned light industrial, with eight shipping containers next to an Oncor substation. Barrio, which bought the property in 2024, would be the final lessee, the Tyler Morning Telegraph and KLTV reported. At a June community meeting, project manager Mitch Brown said it would use a closed-loop system and no city water, create seven to ten jobs and seek no tax abatements. "I live in this neighborhood, I live within a five-minute walk, and I didn't get one flyer, I didn't get one person knocking on my door," resident Amanda Mosley said.

On July 7, 2026, after about three and a half hours and 26 speakers against it, the city's Planning and Zoning Commission voted 5-2 to deny the special use permit, following the staff recommendation. "The plan for the area does not support further intensification of industrial activity," said planning director Kyle Kingma. "We have to consider the overall benefit to our community with this just being seven to 10 jobs when you compare the potential impacts," said Phillip Olivares, who runs the building next door. Commissioners James Wynne and Roy Martinez voted against the denial. In September the Zoning Board of Adjustment ruled unanimously that it had no jurisdiction over Barrio Resources' separate challenge to the city's 2025 ruling that a permit was needed, because the appeal was filed 364 days late, KLTV reported. Barrio still has a timely appeal of the July denial on hold, which would send the decision to the City Council.

At the county level, the Commissioners Court has twice delayed a vote on forming a joint commission with Van Zandt County to study the effects of solar farms, data centers and high-capacity water wells, KLTV reported in May. "This is about protecting our families, our farmland, and our future," said Commissioner Christina Drewry, who backed it. "You either want more government or you want less government," said Commissioner John Moore. "Austin needs to take ownership of this." County Judge Neal Franklin told the crowd, "You must know that we all hear you and we're concerned with the same thing you are."
/data-centers/united-states/texas/smith-.unconfirmed: KLTV describes the facility as '12,500 MW', apparently confusing it with the 12,500-volt service line; the Tyler Morning Telegraph's 12 megawatts is used. KETK's story on a protest at the Smith County Courthouse returned a 35-character shell and is not used. Whether the Commissioners Court ever voted on the joint study commission was not found. The Smith County annex IT data center upgrade (DCD) is a government server room and not included.

paragraphs: Washington County's data center is in Brenham. Viridien, the French earth-science and computing company formerly known as CGG, bought roughly 20 acres at 2602 Longwood Drive from the city's development corporation in a sale that closed in July 2025, after talks that began in April 2022. It plans a $100 million hub for its own high-performance computing, starting with one 40,000-square-foot building and expanding to three, about 45 megawatts at full buildout, KBTX and DCD reported.

The site was moved from FM 332 and FM 389 to address noise concerns, Mayor Atwood Kenjura told KWHI. He said the city had first told the company it would not work because of the water such facilities need; the city says the design uses "significantly less water than many traditional data centers." Power comes from Bluebonnet Electric Cooperative, and Kenjura said the company would provide $20 million to upgrade Bluebonnet's capacity.

Most residents learned of it in January 2026, when the council scheduled a vote to create a reinvestment zone for a tax phase-in. The city said the project "was not rushed, not hidden, and not done behind closed doors" and that it was not a cloud storage site or a crypto mine. "Economic development projects don't always attract attention until people hear a label that sparks concern," said economic development director Teresa Rosales.

On January 8, with more than 100 residents in the room, the council voted down the reinvestment zone, and the room erupted in cheers, KBTX reported. "The lack of transparency just seems like something is wrong," said Taylor Farmer, an environmental consultant who grew up in Brenham. A Change.org petition against the project had more than 1,000 signatures, DCD reported. The vote denies the tax incentive but does not stop the project: the land sale had already closed, and the city said the vote was not about whether the facility comes to Brenham.

In June 2025 Google paid Botetourt County $14 million for 312 acres of the Greenfield industrial park in Daleville, most of the park's remaining land. A March 2026 Army Corps of Engineers notice for "Project Raspberry" showed three data centers, three substations and an office building, Cardinal News reported. The notice said the work would permanently affect about 3 acres of wetlands and almost 7,000 feet of stream channel and clear about 120 acres of forest within the range of the endangered Indiana bat. Google confirmed the campus on March 26. The county expects $30 million a year in tax revenue, more than from any other business, WDBJ reported. Google has committed to at least 50 jobs at each building.

Water drives the fight. The first phase would draw on Carvins Cove, a reservoir serving Roanoke, Botetourt and neighboring localities, under a county agreement with the Western Virginia Water Authority estimating 2 million gallons a day at first and up to 8 million with expansion. The authority says the Carvins Cove plant produces 10 million to 12 million gallons a day and can treat 24 million. Supervisors' chairman Mac Scothorn said the chance of Google actually using 2 million gallons a day was "pretty low". The authority says Google will recycle the water three to five times before sending it to the sewer system. It had expected to need a new regional water source in about 35 years regardless of Google and has started planning early. Google says the 79 megawatts it buys from the Rocky Forge wind farm in the county will not cover the campus. In September, Appalachian Power disclosed that the campus's peak electricity demand will be about 300 megawatts, a figure neither the utility nor Google had made public before; the utility says a nine-figure grid upgrade to serve the project will not raise other customers' rates.

Opposition grew through the spring. Protesters carrying "Water not data" signs came to a March 24 supervisors' meeting, Virginia Business reported. The Southwest Virginia Data Center Transparency Alliance, formed in 2025, said Google's announcement read "like it was written by AI with the prompt to be positive and vague, yet appear genuine." Hundreds came to Google's June open house at Lord Botetourt High School, WVTF reported. "They're concerned about what the noise level's going to be. They're concerned about the water," said Shirley Jarusek of Troutville. Opponent Jessi Bearman claimed Google would use 80 percent of Carvins Cove's output at full capacity. In July Google said the first building would be air-cooled. Its request for up to 8 million gallons a day still awaited the water authority board's approval, and the authority expects refined numbers. The Transparency Alliance's Kathryn Hatam said air cooling "generates more noise, air pollution, and requires more electricity."

Late in July the Board of Supervisors voted to create an independent commission of three to five members from outside the county to study the campus's effects on water, sound and more, and report within six months, WDBJ reported. Residents had wanted the planning commission to do it. "Because I don't trust you all, I don't trust your decision to select people on your own to form this committee to look into the water situation," resident Judy Wilhelm told the board. County Administrator Gary Larrowe, who faced calls for his removal, said: "This is not just a Botetourt County issue. This is not just a Roanoke Valley issue. This is not just a Virginia issue. This is a national issue."

Greensville County lost two prospective data center customers in the spring of 2026. State Finance Secretary Mark Sickles told a Senate committee that Compass Datacenters had stopped looking at sites in Greensville County and Emporia because of uncertainty over Virginia's data center sales-tax exemption; Compass did not say what size projects it had considered. Gov. Abigail Spanberger said the loss "hurts local revenues" and "hurts local services." The General Assembly's eventual compromise kept the tax exemption but added a new energy-consumption tax on data centers.

The county's one project on record, the Mid-Atlantic Advanced Manufacturing Center near Emporia, is a separate, still-proposed industrial site; it is not the Compass project described above, and its backers have not said whether a data center is part of its plans. Officials point to Greensville's 6.6 percent unemployment rate, Emporia's 8.8 percent, and the closed Georgia-Pacific plywood mill as reasons they keep recruiting. "You're talking down in my neck of the woods, a lot of communities are struggling to get by," said Keith Boswell of the Virginia Gateway Region economic development group, who said five data center projects were interested in the region.

Hopewell's only data center prospect is the former Green Plains ethanol plant at 701 South Sixth Avenue, closed since 2018. NS Development Partners bought the 55-acre site in early 2026 and leased about seven acres to an unnamed manufacturer. In July, Volterra Advisors, a Maryland consulting firm, told The Progress-Index it had worked with the property owners on an analysis that found part of the site suited to a small data center of about 50,000 to 70,000 square feet running on about 20 megawatts. For comparison, the paper noted that Google's three data centers under construction in nearby Chesterfield County will draw 200 to 300 megawatts. "There's potential to re-use the natural gas lines," Volterra founder Jeramy Utara said. He blamed excess noise at data centers "on a few bad actors" in the industry and said nothing like that would happen in Hopewell.

The first report said Volterra's case study had been done with the city, and Hopewell disputed that. In a July 13 statement, city spokesperson Kyle English said the city "did not commission, participate in, or conduct any case study regarding the development of the property." He said the city had received formal inquiries in March 2025 and May 2026 about whether a data center was an allowable use at the site, and that no proposal is considered until an application is filed. The Progress-Index reported that the case study had been taken down from Volterra's website. No application has been reported.
/data-centers/united-states/virginia/hop.unconfirmed: WRIC's story, in which search snippets say both the city and Volterra denied coordinating, returned a 35-character shell; Volterra's own denial is therefore not stated. The 'early 2026' purchase date is inferred from the Progress-Index's 'about four months ago' in a July 2026 story.

paragraphs: Prince Edward County spent six years preparing for a data center. In 2020 it gave its Industrial Development Authority $1.5 million to buy 280 acres near Farmville, made data centers a by-right use in the C-1 zone and rezoned the land, since named the Heartland Innovative Technology (HIT) Park. It later cut its tax on data center equipment from $4.50 to $1.00 per $100 of value, DCD and The Farmville Herald reported. In January 2025 supervisors approved selling the park to AVAIO Digital for $12.2 million. Under the agreement the company would invest $800 million to $2.4 billion depending on what it builds. The county's IDA would build about $12.6 million of water infrastructure, the Town of Farmville about $8.1 million of sewer, and the county the road improvements. In April 2026 the sale deadline was extended six months while officials waited on Dominion Energy to say what power it could deliver.

Opposition arrived once the contract did. More than a dozen residents spoke at the June 9 supervisors' meeting and eleven more on August 11. "We elect our representatives so that we can trust them to make good decisions without us looking over their shoulders. We're here because you made some bad decisions and now we have to look over your shoulders," said Courtney Faller, the Hampden-Sydney College swim coach. Greg Phipps, who lives about half a mile from the site, asked the board to "pause this project, open up a fully transparent public review." County Administrator Doug Stanley said every step had followed public hearings, that no site plan had been filed, and that staff were drafting extra rules on noise, buffers, lighting, generators and water. Supervisor David Emert told the crowd to "show up from the beginning." Supervisor Cannon Watson said the county was "beholden to Dominion who is moving at a snail's pace to say yes or no that they could provide the power." "If they say no, it's over," he said.

Board chairman Harrison Jones, who said nearly two dozen family members live within 2.5 miles of the park, wrote that a data center "could provide so much funding that it could replace 30% of current revenue" and that he "firmly believe[s] that a data center would benefit, and not harm, our home." At its information meeting in late August, AVAIO's Kevin Murphy said the "Project Pegasus" campus would be five buildings on about 200 acres, a nearly $5 billion investment with about 150 permanent jobs, and "several years away from any groundbreaking." The company said it had no tenant because it had no permit or power commitment, that it would use closed-loop cooling and up to about 6,000 gallons of water a day per building for sanitary needs, and that environmental studies had not begun. Its representatives acknowledged that nondisclosure agreements may be required and that the company could qualify for grants or rebates.
/data-centers/united-states/virginia/pri.unconfirmed: The Herald gives the AVAIO information meeting as Aug. 27 in its preview and Aug. 17 in its report; 'late August' is used.
