AVAIO's water and jobs figures are company statements, attributed. Citizen Portal's account of the June meeting is not used. Site data: the only project mapped to this page is the Prince William Digital Gateway, placed at a Virginia centroid in Prince Edward County by a geocoding fallback; it does not belong here, and the HIT Park project is not on the map.

paragraphs: A QTS-backed data center campus near Kearneysville straddles the Jefferson-Berkeley county line; 191 acres on the Jefferson County side are zoned industrial, but no site plans have been filed with the county planning office. IB10 Martinsburg LLC bought the parcels in July 2024, and the project has access to a natural gas pipeline and two high-capacity transmission lines. On the Berkeley County side, planners approved a concept plan in March 2025 for two buildings on 90 acres, reached from Charles Town Road. "We are in the initial stages of planning," a QTS representative said.

Jefferson County has been writing rules for data centers rather than reviewing this project. In June 2025 the planning commission scheduled a draft ordinance covering data centers and solar for public comment at its July and August 2025 meetings, and it directed staff to cap public comment at 90 minutes per agenda item. The Jefferson County Foundation said the commission had "usurped the processes" needed to change its rules. West Virginia's 2025 law on "high-impact" data centers already limits how much counties can regulate certified projects.
The public comment sessions on the draft ordinance were scheduled for July and August 2025; no result has been published.

Monongalia County has no privately proposed data center of the size drawing scrutiny elsewhere in West Virginia; the county's only tracked project is the federal government's own. The National Energy Technology Laboratory is building a Computational Science & Engineering Center on its Morgantown campus, consolidating the lab's existing data centers into one building with a server hall for its Joule supercomputer, NETL says; construction is underway. County Commissioner Sean Sikora told The Dominion Post in August 2026 that no private developer has offered terms worth taking: "I have to ask whether the community hosting these hundreds of acres of infrastructure and absorbing its impacts receives an adequate return, and I haven't been shown a model yet that tells me that."

Sikora and Delegate Evan Hansen, D-Monongalia, both criticized House Bill 2014, the 2025 state law under which certified high-impact data centers are exempt from county zoning, noise rules and building permits. Hansen said the law takes most tax revenue from the host county, though 30 percent stays there. Sikora said a separate 2009 law taxing high-technology property at 5 percent salvage value could cost the county about 38.5 percent of the property tax it would otherwise collect if such a project came.

The county is still drawn into the state's data center build-out. In July 2025 its commission voted to oppose NextEra's MidAtlantic Resiliency Link, a proposed 105-mile power line through Monongalia and Preston counties to a data center in Frederick County, Virginia. "They want to shove this thing down our throat and say oh by the way you also get to pay for it and you don't get benefit from it," said commission president Jeff Arnett. FirstEnergy has also begun permitting a 1,200-megawatt gas plant at Maidsville, beside the Fort Martin coal plant, to meet demand a company vice president said could come from a single large customer.

Menomonie's City Council voted 8-3 in August 2025 to annex 324 acres along County Highway B and rezone it industrial for a data center proposed by Balloonist LLC, a company that has not said who would operate it. The city's fact sheet described a $1.6 billion project with up to 1,000 construction jobs. Mayor Randy Knaack put incentive talks on pause weeks later, but Balloonist bought the land anyway, and current Mayor Matthew Crowe confirmed the purchase in June 2026.

The city has been writing zoning rules for data centers ever since. It introduced a first draft of an I-4 zoning ordinance on August 3, 2026, with no vote taken, and a second draft on September 8, again with no vote taken. Council held a special session on September 15 with an outside attorney to discuss the draft; no date for a vote has been set.
Crowe has twice declined to meet with Balloonist before the ordinance is finished, "to avoid being unduly influenced." Once the ordinance is adopted, Balloonist could apply to rezone its land to I-4.

Grant County's data center arrived and left without anyone learning who was behind it. In the fall of 2025, out-of-state developers who had been scouting northern Illinois for a crypto project saw the Cardinal-Hickory Creek transmission line crossing into Grant County. "There's a chunk of power there, Ron, and we need to grab it before someone else does," county economic development director Ron Brisbois recalled them saying, Wisconsin Watch reported. They floated a $1 billion to $2 billion hyperscale campus of about 500 acres near the town of Cassville (population 400), at least three times larger than any development in the county. Brisbois estimated it would need 400 to 500 megawatts and produce about 50 jobs and $5.5 million a year in property taxes. He went public in December but never named the developers.

Opposition built through the spring. More than 600 people came to a March event in Potosi with the comedian Charlie Berens, and Pete Moris of the "No Data Centers in the Driftless" group helped lead the effort. Moris said not being told who the developer or the end user was felt "scary." In the town of Cassville, which had no zoning, residents voted 44-0 at a town meeting to tell their board to stop the project, and in April the board passed an ordinance banning data centers for up to two years. The town's attorney, Eric Hagen, said the developer was "looking for the lowest-hanging fruit with the least amount of regulations." "This is the Driftless area for Christ's sakes," said resident John Hawn. Other Grant County towns and the County Board followed with moratoriums of their own, Wisconsin Watch reported.

After a March call about incentives, Brisbois told the developers a tax increment district probably was not legally possible for a town, and he later attributed their silence to the lack of local tax incentives. "It's gone dead quiet," Brisbois said in April. By June he was still calling without an answer, and his daughters told him he was being "ghosted." "This data center project is going to be located somewhere," he had written to his board. "If it's going to be somewhere, it should be here."
/data-centers/united-states/wisconsin/gr.unconfirmed: The Telegraph Herald's report of the County Board's unanimous 12-month moratorium on hyperscale data centers in unincorporated areas was not read; only Wisconsin Watch's statement that the County Board adopted a moratorium is used. Beetown's interim ordinance and Bloomington's consideration of one appeared only in search snippets and are not stated. WEAU's June Berens event was in western Wisconsin, not Grant County.

paragraphs: Kewaunee County's data center prospect ended in a handshake. The developer Cloverleaf Infrastructure had looked at land in the town of Carlton, home of the shuttered Kewaunee Power Station on Lake Michigan, a county where cattle outnumber people by nearly 5 to 1. In late 2025 it dropped the idea after residents opposed it, Cloverleaf and town officials told Wisconsin Watch in January 2026. "The town chairperson said, 'I don't support data centers. I don't think this is a good fit,'" said Cloverleaf's chief development officer, Aaron Bilyeu. "We shook hands and said 'thank you.'" Town Chairman David Hardtke, who had pushed back for months, put it plainly: "People in the town of Carlton do not want the AI (data) center." Cloverleaf also dropped a proposal in Greenleaf, in neighboring Brown County, after an outcry, and Bilyeu said the company was still looking for a site in northeast Wisconsin. "We're not the only ones looking for data center sites in the area," he said.

Carlton's position is shaped by the power plant it hopes to get back. The Kewaunee station closed in 2013, and the town had run its budget off its utility taxes, Hardtke told WPR. Its owner, EnergySolutions, has filed with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to bring new nuclear generation to the site, with construction not expected before the early 2030s. Hardtke supports it, since spent fuel already sits on the property, but not what might follow. "They're just crawling out of the woodwork right now, trying to eat up the farmland," he said of developers. "If Carlton is hosting the power plant, we don't have to host everything, so they can locate their Cloverleaf and other data centers someplace else," he told Spectrum News. Not everyone agreed: resident Dan Giannotti told Wisconsin Watch the county had stagnated since the plant closed and that an employer like that would bring new homes and businesses.

The Wisconsin Rapids paper mill closed in 2020 with almost 1,000 jobs lost and was torn down in 2025. A first data center plan for the site, a 20-megawatt project from Digital Power Optimization, was cancelled in July 2025. A second developer, PNK Group, has been weighing the site since December 2025 through an entity called PCH WI Holdings LLC; the city says it has signed no nondisclosure agreements and has no financial partnership with any developer.

Opposition built through 2026. In April the Common Council adopted zoning standards confining data centers to the mill site's industrial district. On August 10 the Planning Commission voted unanimously to recommend a one-year moratorium on new data centers to the Common Council.

After more than three hours of public comment on September 16, the commission unanimously rejected the conditional use permit for DC Rapids LLC's roughly 200-acre campus at 950 Fourth Avenue North, the site PNK is proposing, and sent both the denial and the moratorium recommendation to the Common Council. "We don't know how to be proactive necessarily because nobody's really ever done; there's no playbook on this," said Mayor Matt Zacher, who now backs the moratorium.

In June 2026, meeting in Lyman, the County Commission unanimously granted a conditional use permit for Prometheus Hyperscale's 1.25-gigawatt campus on 506 acres of the Thornock family's ranch near Evanston, following its planning and zoning committee's recommendation, Cowboy State Daily reported. Public comment ran roughly even for and against. Prometheus says the campus will run as a fully islanded microgrid on its own natural gas engines and turbines, off the public grid, DCD reported; the company was known as Wyoming Hyperscale Whitebox when it first planned a 120MW campus on the site in 2020. Founder Trenton Thornock said its closed-loop cooling would draw no water from the county system and use about as much water as 15 homes for bathrooms and offices. He said the company sought no tax abatements. "I didn't ask for any handouts," he said. Supporters cite about 3,800 construction jobs and about 200 permanent ones. Conditions on the permit include dust and noise limits, closed-loop cooling and a requirement that electric rates not be adversely affected.

Opponents drew on the county's history. Petition organizer Alex Rossi pointed to an Evanston deal for a brewery in the Roundhouse that was sold as worth $2.8 million over ten years and still had not opened five years later. "So my concern is, say something goes a little south for Prometheus," he said. "And we end up holding the bag again as residents." Attorney Parker Jackson urged the commission to treat the project as a test of property rights: "I think we have to have a level playing field, both for property owners and for businesses." In July three residents filed a petition in court for administrative review of the approval, alleging unadvertised meetings and undisclosed family conflicts of interest, which county officials denied, and arguing an environmental study of the cooling system was needed. On August 17 Judge James Kaste dismissed it, finding the petitioners had not answered a motion to dismiss in time or shown how they would be harmed. Prometheus president Trevor Neilson called it "a really frivolous appeal". He said the company's $16 billion investment in Uinta, matched by a second campus planned in Natrona County, would raise county tax revenue by about 70 percent.
/data-centers/united-states/wyoming/uint.unconfirmed: Job, investment and tax-revenue figures are the company's and are attributed. Reports disagree on the number of permit conditions (a snippet said 15; Neilson spoke of '30 or so'), so none is given. Cowboy State Daily's May forum story, WyoFile, KPCW and the Uinta County Herald explainer were fetched but not needed. Whether the separate power-infrastructure permit was approved at the late-August commission meeting was not confirmed from text read.

paragraphs: AdaniConneX is a 50/50 joint venture between Adani Enterprises, part of India's Adani Group, and the US operator EdgeConneX. It was announced in February 2021 with a goal of 1GW of hyperscale capacity across India, DCD reported. Its first campus, in Chennai, opened with a 17MW first phase and will reach 33MW; it has since worked on sites in Noida, where the construction site had a small fire, Vizag, Hyderabad, Pune and Mumbai. In April 2024 it signed up to $1.44 billion of sustainability-linked construction financing with eight international banks, bringing its financing pool to $1.65 billion, Business Standard reported. DCD's coverage of that deal noted that the Adani Group had come under fire in 2023 after the short-seller Hindenburg Research alleged stock manipulation, accounting fraud and money laundering, claims the conglomerate denied.

Its largest commitment is in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh. Adani Group broke ground on May 3, 2023 on an over-200MW "Integrated Data Center and Technology Business Park" in the Madhurawada area, to be hosted by AdaniConneX and powered by 100 percent renewable energy. Then-Chief Minister Jagan Mohan Reddy said it would bring a submarine cable from Singapore, and his successor, N. Chandrababu Naidu, has promoted the state as "India's premier investment destination, powered by speed, trust, and ease of doing business." On April 28, 2026, Google broke ground on its $15 billion AI hub in Vizag, three campuses approaching a gigawatt in combined capacity, DCD and CRN Asia reported. AdaniConneX and Nxtra by Airtel are to build and operate those campuses, with Google running its AI and cloud workloads on them. The Adani Group said in December 2025 it would invest up to $5 billion in the Vizag campus, which is due to be commissioned by July 2028.

Bulk Infrastructure, a Norwegian data center operator, has closed a €410 million loan to keep building its N01 campus in Vennesla municipality, just outside Kristiansand in the Agder region, the site CoreWeave chose for an Nvidia GB200 NVL72 cluster. The loan, arranged by ABN Amro, Citibank Europe and Nordea, is secured against N01's first phase and will pay for continued expansion and refinance existing debt. "This financing marks a significant milestone for our robust platform to meet fast-growing customer demand for AI training and inference," chief executive Jon Gravråk said.

The campus sits on a three-square-kilometer site next to a transformer station, with 400 megawatts of power secured and room to expand to 1 gigawatt, DCD reported. Construction began in 2014; Bulk opened a 12-megawatt facility there in 2023 and broke ground on a 42-megawatt facility in January 2024, designed for high-density GPU and CPU equipment, which is the building CoreWeave announced in March 2025 for one of the largest Nvidia AI deployments in Europe. Bulk said it was also working with regional and national grid companies to add 300 megawatts of capacity in 2026.

Bulk also runs the Oslo Internet Exchange, a former printing press that opened as a data center in 2014. It took full ownership in January 2022 by buying out the hydropower company Akershus Energi, and added three data halls that doubled its capacity to 14 megawatts. It also operates a site in Esbjerg, Denmark, and holds land for future expansion in Arendal, Norway.

Green Mountain's biggest project is a TikTok data center campus at Heggvin, between Hamar and Løten in Norway, part of TikTok's "Project Clover" effort to keep European user data in Europe. The OSL-Hamar campus is planned as five buildings of 30MW each; TikTok has contracted three, with an option on the rest, and has already taken over the first hall, NRK reported. Norway's government found no grounds to block the deal but placed Green Mountain under the country's security law.

The energy regulator NVE ordered Green Mountain to stop building the campus transformer station because its license had not yet been approved, and said preparatory work already done had broken the law, Kom24 reported. CEO Svein Atle Hagaseth told Hamar Arbeiderblad the company believed it had done what it was allowed to do, but stopped work immediately once NVE disagreed. Løten Green Party council member Jon Lurås objected that it was wrong to spend Norway's power on TikTok.

Green Mountain, founded in 2009, was bought by Israel's Azrieli Group from Smedvig in 2021 for about NIS 2.8 billion ($849 million), DCD reported. Its flagship is DC1-Stavanger, built into a mountain inside a former NATO ammunition store; it also runs sites in Rjukan and outside Oslo, and has since expanded to Romford outside London and announced a campus near Frankfurt. It has also planned a campus of up to eight halls in Kalberg, near Stavanger in Time municipality, for an international client.

In July 2026 Calcalist reported Azrieli had hired Goldman Sachs to find an investor for about a 20 percent stake in Green Mountain, for roughly 1 billion euros at a valuation of at least 5 billion euros; some market participants believed the TikTok contract had put investors off, which the company denied. In December 2025 Green Mountain signed an 80MW campus deal with another international customer, its largest since TikTok.

Canberra has about 15 data centers, mostly on industrial estates and one in suburban Bruce, and more are coming. The largest operator, Canberra-founded CDC Data Centres, runs eight data centers on four campuses in the ACT, serving federal agencies and national security clients. In September 2026 it lodged a development application for Beard 2, a $200 million, three-story building with 12 data halls and on-site emergency generators, next to its Beard building, which is still being fitted out and will have 40 megawatts of power. The government says another data center may be extended in Hume.

Canberra has seen little of the opposition found elsewhere. Operators credit closed-loop cooling that does not draw on the water supply and the territory's 100% renewable electricity. Chief Minister Andrew Barr says there is no need to pause new data centers because ACT rules likely already meet proposed national standards, and he wants any new large power user to "bring with them a renewable energy solution." He has also said the ACT's water supply can cope for another 10 to 15 years, after which the government faces a decision.

After national cabinet agreed on data center standards in August 2026, Barr announced an ACT framework setting where data centers may be built and how proposals are assessed, with protections for homes and water. The government aims to release a draft in early 2027.

Queensland's data center story changed in August 2026, when Singapore-based developer Zerra DC filed plans for what would be Australia's largest data center: the Western Downs Digital Park, a 2.16-gigawatt campus on a 725-hectare former cattle feedlot near Dalby, about 250 kilometers northwest of Brisbane. The developer says it would connect directly to the high-voltage grid at the nearby Braemar substation and could take four to six years to build. On September 16, 2026, the state government told Parliament that Anthropic had signed a lease to use part of the site to run its Claude system, starting in 2027, pending federal foreign-investment approval.

Water is the question locals raise first. The development application says construction would need about 522,000 liters a day; Zerra DC says the finished campus would draw 25.5 million liters a year, mostly from rainwater and recycling, with groundwater only as a last resort. Ian Wright, an environmental scientist at Western Sydney University, told the ABC the numbers sounded "too good to be true" but added, "it looks like they've done their homework." Toowoomba Regional Council has passed a motion to keep data centers away from drinking-water sources.

The bigger fight is over power. Liza Balmain of the anti-gas group Save Our Darling Downs said the community had been "asking for the brakes to be put on," and is "deeply concerned" the campus could run on gas-fired power. The Climate Council's Amanda McKenzie said it could use three times the power of Brisbane's 1.4 million residents and push wholesale prices up by at least 13%. Premier David Crisafulli called the project "a major win" that would create jobs and lower power prices; the federal government wants new data centers tied to new renewable power, which Queensland has refused.

Brisbane's only tracked data centers are NEXTDC's B1 and B2 and its Sunshine Coast site, all far smaller than the proposed Western Downs project. What happens next: the Western Downs Regional Council is assessing Zerra DC's application, a process the ABC reported could take years; the Foreign Investment Review Board must approve Anthropic's lease; and Canberra has pledged national data center rules for early 2027.

Digital Realty, which bought Interxion, runs two data centers in Vienna, VIE1 and VIE2, including the one in Floridsdorf that Wien Energie calls the largest in Austria. In 2020 Interxion bought a 22,000-square-meter plot next to the campus for a new center of up to 40 megawatts of computing power, and Microsoft announced an Azure cloud region for Austria at the Federal Chancellery. Any new or substantially modernized data center in the city now faces heat-reuse rules that took effect in July 2026.

Under Vienna's Energy Law Amendment Act 2026, a data center drawing more than 1 megawatt must weigh, before it is built, modernized or switched on, whether its waste heat can go into the district heating network, working with the heating operator. Building one also generally needs a permit, unless its heat is used, according to the law firm E+H. The law has no transition period.

In Floridsdorf, Wien Energie spent about €3.5 million on three 1-megawatt heat pumps that take heat from the data center's roughly 26°C cooling water and pipe it underground to Klinik Floridsdorf, an 800-bed hospital next door, covering 50 to 70 percent of its heating. In its bid for one of the EU's AI "gigafactories," worth up to €5 billion, Vienna proposed a center whose server heat would feed the city network; Stefan Gara, a Neos member of the Vienna state parliament, estimates that could heat about 200,000 households.

Heilongjiang's main data center is China Mobile's Harbin campus in the Hanan industrial new town, and it has been growing. Its AI computing cluster of about 18,000 Chinese-made accelerator cards, built with Huawei, went into service in 2024. Two more buildings, B04 and B05, designed for more than 61 megawatts of computing load, were scheduled to go into production by the end of June 2026; no update has been published since.

The province only entered the business in 2024 and is selling cold weather and cheap power. At a June 2025 investment event in Harbin it said data centers could get electricity for as little as 0.36 yuan per kilowatt-hour without subsidy, and pointed to winters of five to six months and an average temperature of 3.5°C. It is planning a computing park in Harbin's Pingfang District with a dedicated wind and solar power network.

China Mobile's campus has more than 160,000 square meters built and room for 18,000 racks; its customers include the provincial government cloud, banks, Baidu, Alibaba, Tencent and ByteDance. Others have followed. The Harbin Digital Longjiang AI computing center opened its first phase in 2024, and construction began that April on the 875 million yuan Jing'an Huili Northeast Asia Intelligent Computing Center on Zhigu Avenue in Harbin New Area, whose first phase was due to open that year.

The biggest data center announced inside Berlin is Virtus's BERLIN1 campus in Marienpark: four buildings for cloud, government and business customers, which the British operator said would open in 2026. Its waste heat is to go into a heating network run by Marienpark's developers, Investa and the gas utility GASAG. NTT also runs a data center in the city.

Power is what limits new ones. About three years ago data center operators started asking the city's grid company, Stromnetz Berlin, for connections of around 100 megawatts each, more than the peak demand of the whole city of Potsdam. The company paused large requests and now shares out the little spare capacity once a year, while holding power back so households can still connect car chargers and heat pumps. "Had we not changed the process and adopted a moratorium last year, our capacity for large connection requests would now be exhausted," said Kerstin Niemeier of Stromnetz Berlin.

Only about 350 megawatts remain for large users, in parts of the south of the city and at one point in the north. Stromnetz Berlin plans to invest almost €3 billion by 2029 and to double its grid capacity to about 4.5 gigawatts within ten years. The Berlin Senate says it wants smaller data centers built into the city that can feed existing heat networks.

Hafnarfjörður has Iceland's oldest dedicated data center. The atNorth facility on Steinhella began as Thor Data Center, formally opened in Hafnarfjörður as the first specialized Icelandic data center, with the Norwegian software company Opera as its largest customer, the local paper Fjarðarfréttir reported. Through a later chain of owners it became part of Advania Data Centers, which renamed itself atNorth in December 2020. DCD lists the site as atNorth's 3.2MW ICE01. In an interview with Fjarðarfréttir, atNorth chief executive Eyjólfur Magnús Kristinsson, a Hafnarfjörður native, said the roughly 2,600-square-metre building was essentially full, with space held for a European bank, and that there were no plans to expand it. Because the site is small, atNorth has to buy its power through the distributor HS Veitur rather than directly from the national grid operator Landsnet, which raises the price considerably, he said. He called that the "Achilles heel" of a location in a green neighbourhood. He said no bitcoin mining happens there, because it would never pay there, though it can still pay at the larger Reykjanesbær site. The company's growth has instead gone to its much larger campuses at Reykjanesbær and Akureyri.

Those campuses are where Iceland's data center boom is happening. atNorth said in November 2024 that it was investing 41.2 billion krónur in expanding them, with customers adding nearly 300 billion krónur of equipment, mbl.is reported. In September 2026, Iceland Review noted, atNorth changed hands in a $4 billion deal, days after Statistics Iceland reported that data-center-related investment had reached a record high even as GDP contracted. Iceland's industry spent years dominated by crypto mining; a 2018 KPMG report found 90 percent of the country's data center capacity mined crypto. atNorth told DCD it was no longer taking new crypto customers.
/data-centers/iceland/hafnarfjar-arkaups.unconfirmed: Icelandic sources are translated. The Fjarðarfréttir interview's date was not in the text read, so its capacity and staffing figures (about 2MW, about 15 staff) are not stated as current. DCD places ICE01 in 'Reykjavik'; the address is in Hafnarfjörður in the capital region. Borealis and Verne are also listed as operating in Hafnarfjörður by listing sites, but no reporting on their Hafnarfjörður sites was read, so they are not described. The Iceland Review piece is a first-person essay; only its factual reporting is used.

paragraphs: Liguria's place in the data center map comes from Genoa's role as a landing point for undersea cables. In February 2021 Equinix and Vodafone announced the GN1 data center in Genoa to land the 2Africa cable, which reached GN1 in April 2022, Submarine Networks reported. GN1 is linked directly to Equinix's Milan facilities. In February 2026 the Unitirreno cable was completed: more than 1,000 kilometres from Mazara del Vallo in Sicily via Rome-Fiumicino and Olbia to Genoa, with 24 fibre pairs and 624 Tbps of total capacity, Il Sole 24 Ore and La Voce di Genova reported. It cost €80 million, and it comes ashore through a one-kilometre bore pipe under the seabed and reaches the Lagaccio Digital Hub through an existing urban tunnel, where the landing station is integrated with a neutral data center. "There is the need to balance the weight of Marseille, which has a very high concentration of cables," said Renato Brunetti, chief executive of Unitirreno and Unidata. "If an accident happens in Marseille, the internet stops in the whole of Europe, if not the whole world." Regional president Marco Bucci said Liguria "can truly become Italy's data port".

The region's own data center belongs to Liguria Digitale, which runs the servers for Liguria's public administration. After two years and €3 million of renovation it reopened with 2,000 square metres and more than 4,000 virtual and physical servers, DCD reported. Not everyone is comfortable with the direction. In a September 2026 dossier for the Ligurian outlet Trucioli, a local critic argued that GN1 and facilities like it are a new and heavy item in the regional energy budget that the region's PEAR 2030 energy plan does not address. The critic noted that Bucci, as mayor of Genoa, had backed the GN1 project.
/data-centers/italy/liguria/.unconfirmed: Italian quotations are translated; Brunetti's is from Il Sole 24 Ore's English edition. The Trucioli piece is an opinion dossier and is attributed as such. No hyperscale data center proposal in Liguria was found. Quadrivium Digital's GEN01 appeared only on listing sites and is not described.

paragraphs: Seika, the town where Kyoto Prefecture's data centers cluster, has decided it has enough. The town said it will in principle stop recruiting new data centers to its science-city district, citing their heavy electricity use, the environmental concern from large emergency generators, and the fact that, unlike manufacturing, they do not bring many jobs. Exceptions would go only to facilities that fit the surroundings and serve as research and development infrastructure; the town said it is giving advance guidance to already-approved projects so environmental problems do not arise. Nearby in Kyotanabe, the logistics developer Prologis said in June it was considering a data center or warehouse on about 95,000 square meters next to its existing Prologis Park, with construction around 2026 to 2027.

Seika sits in the Kansai Science City (Keihanna) research district on the borders of Kyoto, Osaka and Nara. On April 9, 2026, NTT DATA opened its Keihanna OSK11 there, a four-storey, air-cooled building with 30MW of IT capacity, NTT's 14th data center in Japan. The "Osaka" names on two of the town's other sites, STACK's KIX01 and Kansai Electric Power CyrusOne's OSK1, refer to the wider Kansai region the campuses serve; both are also built in Seika, inside Kyoto Prefecture, on land including a lease from the ATR research institute. Kansai Electric Power CyrusOne, a 50/50 joint venture between the utility and the US operator CyrusOne, broke ground in September 2024 and is due to begin operating in fiscal 2027, the Denki Shimbun reported; the venture aims for 900 megawatts of total capacity within about ten years.

Luxembourg's biggest data center story is Google's plan for Bissen, under discussion since 2016. On January 13, 2025, the Bissen council approved the site's special development plan, but Google still has no building permit. Mayor David Viaggi said: "The absence of a building permit still raises questions about whether the project will actually be carried out." No newer update on the permit has been published.

Water is the sticking point. The environmental group Mouvement écologique says construction cannot begin until environmental permits are granted, which have not happened, and puts water use at 51 cubic meters a day during construction and 11 once running. "The municipality of Bissen has a responsibility not to present its citizens with a fait accompli," the group said. Google has agreed to pay €13.5 million for road and network access and about €1.5 million for an agricultural path, money the community keeps even if the project is dropped.

The country's existing capacity is mostly state-linked. LuxConnect runs three Tier IV data centers plus a fourth in Bissen that hosts MeluXina, a €30 million supercomputer funded by the EU and Luxembourg. Its sites run on renewable power, with server heat piped to a new neighborhood in Bettembourg. The private Portus Data Center at Cloche d'Or, open since 2009, has said it plans to add more space in the years ahead.

Negeri Sembilan has two large data center campuses under way and a third under discussion. At Springhill Industrial Park in Port Dickson, Gamuda bought 389 acres of farmland and has agreed to sell it to Pearl Computing, a Google affiliate, for RM455.2 million, while doing the earthworks and building a water treatment plant for the site. Near Seremban, Vena Nexus broke ground in January 2026 on the Nexus Yang campus at NS Semiconductor Valley, planned for about 350 megawatts of power and due for completion in early 2027.

Water is the state's condition for these projects. Menteri Besar Aminuddin Harun told the state assembly in April 2025 that the state would assess new proposals carefully because data centers use so much water. Gamuda's treatment plant at Springhill will produce 65 million liters a day, with a quarter reserved for local households and the plant owned by the state. Analysts estimated the Springhill land could hold 700 to 1,000 megawatts; Google has not said how large its data centers there will be.

Two smaller plans are also on record. Aminuddin said US investors are developing a green data center in Nilai. The Malaysian developer Tanco signed a nonbinding agreement with China Mobile International to consider a 50-megawatt data center in Port Dickson, DCD reported.

Innlandet's data center is Green Mountain's OSL-Hamar campus at Heggvin business park, straddling the Hamar and Løten municipalities, built for TikTok. It was announced in March 2023 and has five 30MW buildings. Green Mountain says it invested about 9.7 billion kroner in the first three, which TikTok uses to store and process data for its European users under Project Clover. According to a Menon Economics report commissioned by Green Mountain, 220 people work there permanently, and TikTok invested about 30 billion kroner in servers and equipment. The first building was handed over in November 2023 after Hamar and Løten approved the development the previous autumn. "This is the biggest industrial investment in Innlandet ever," said the regional development agency Hamarregionen Utvikling.

The power it takes has been the argument. Green Mountain's own figures put the campus at 150MW, and at full capacity it could use nearly 1 percent of the electricity produced in Norway, NRK reported; the company told E24 real use is normally 50 to 70 percent of that. "There is a power surplus in the region," chief executive Svein Atle Hagaseth said. "They will take power that will be in short supply for the production of something that is not socially useful," said Frode Alfheim, leader of the LO union Industri Energi. Red Party MP Sofie Marhaug called it "a waste of power" that should go to climate-friendly industry, "not TikTok cat videos". The government decided it had no grounds to intervene but placed Green Mountain under Norway's security law. Innlandet's grid is now tight: at a regional meeting, Statnett and the grid company Elvia said capacity was essentially full, with transformer upgrades planned for 2026 and 2027 and a move from 300kV to 420kV lines by 2035, the Innlandet branch of Friends of the Earth Norway reported.
/data-centers/norway/innlandet/.unconfirmed: Norwegian quotations are translated. Investment, jobs and ripple-effect figures come from Green Mountain's press release of a report it commissioned, attributed. The Naturvernforbundet piece is the environmental group's account of a Statnett and Elvia briefing, not a news report. The Hamarregionen Utvikling quote comes from the same press release.

paragraphs: Gangwon Province is selling itself as Korea's AI data center province on the strength of power and land. The province estimates it generates about 36 terawatt-hours of electricity a year against about 17 consumed locally, a self-sufficiency rate above 210 percent, and the Bank of Korea's Gangwon office judged its sites competitive for AI data centers, the Hankook Ilbo reported in July 2026. The biggest project is on the east coast: in July the province, Donghae city and GS signed an agreement for an AI data center campus at the Bukpyeong No. 2 industrial complex, 2.4 gigawatts by 2029, with the first 1.2 GW due by 2028. Kangwon Ilbo reported the investment at 30 trillion won, or up to 120 trillion won including GPUs and memory. The site sits beside GS Donghae Electric's 1.19 GW power plant, and GS E&C was targeting a groundbreaking in early October, the Korea Herald reported. Governor Woo Sang-ho promised "maximum administrative support". SK's planned AI data center in Gangneung has a problem: there are no 345kV facilities to supply it, and the province has set up a task force with the government and KEPCO to find an answer.

Chuncheon, the provincial capital, is building around cold water. Samsung C&T has applied to build a modular AI data center of an initial 2.4MW, with room to grow, on a 37,475-square-metre site next to Samsung SDS's existing data center in Chiljeon-dong, which Samsung SDS would operate, The Elec reported. Samsung SDS called it a pilot. The city is also developing an 800,000-square-metre "hydrothermal energy cluster" that would pipe deep water released from the Soyang Dam, 6 to 7°C all year, to cool data centers, YTN reported. Because large companies have asked to buy the whole site, Chuncheon has lobbied the government to let it pick investors by evaluation rather than by lottery. A province official told the Hankook Ilbo that water supply had been the biggest problem two or three years ago but that improving technology had eased the worry.
/data-centers/south-korea/gangwon-do/.unconfirmed: Korean sources are translated. The Hankook Ilbo writes the power figures as '36TW' and '17TW'; they are annual generation and consumption and are given here as terawatt-hours. GS's investment figures are the company's and the province's. Naver's GAK Chuncheon data center, long established in the city, is not described because no news report on it was read. No local opposition in Gangwon was found in the reporting read.

paragraphs: Gyeonggi Province's data center fights center on Goyang, where data centers are planned in five neighborhoods: Deogi-dong, Munbong-dong, Siksa-dong, Sari-hyeon-dong and Hyang-dong. Elsewhere in the province, Keppel said on June 9, 2026 that it had bought land in Ansan for a 60-megawatt data center that already has construction permits and power approvals and is due to open by 2030.

In Siksa-dong, a 16-story data center is planned on a 27,000-square-meter site, about four soccer fields. Kang Soon-mo, who chairs the residents' emergency committee, told the Hankook Ilbo it would sit 54 meters from the apartment boundary, with an elementary school of 1,000 pupils less than 200 meters away. The developer applied for a building permit in September 2024 and passed the city's planning and building reviews with conditions, but has not broken ground. The Goyang city council passed a resolution against the project in February 2025.

On November 25, 2024 about 100 residents of Munbong, Sari-hyeon and Siksa rallied at Goyang City Hall, saying a nursing home with about 800 residents and a church visited by about 3,000 people sit near the Munbong site. At Deogi-dong, Magna PFV, a GS Group construction affiliate, had its five-story data center permit nearly canceled after almost 6,000 residents objected, then won an appeal to Gyeonggi Province and was cleared to build on the original site, DCD reported.

In Gwacheon, data centers are planned on five business parcels in the Jueam district; residents say the site is 25 meters from an apartment complex due to open in September 2028. Korean building law treats data centers as broadcasting and communications facilities, so neighbors get no advance notice of a permit. Of 112 data centers built or under construction nationwide, only 26 ever held a resident briefing or public hearing.

Much of Taiwan's new data center building is in Taoyuan. On Baoshi Street in Guishan, behind the Hongbao residential community, Vantage's TPE11 is finished and Keppel and DDSP's 80-megawatt Westwood campus is going up on more than four hectares of hillside, The Reporter found in April 2026. Microsoft opened a 40-megawatt data center in Guishan in 2024 and is building a 50-megawatt one in Luzhu.

"This project involves two companies, and from what I've heard both are foreign firms," said Chen Wen-ching, chief of Xinling Village, where the hills once held a coal mine and brick kilns. The Baoshi Street projects sit right beside homes but have not triggered large protests, The Reporter said. Chunghwa Telecom has also been building a five-story, NT$1.59 billion data center in Taoyuan since 2022.

Taoyuan sits on the line that shapes the market: since September 2023 Taipower has not approved data centers above 5 megawatts north of Taoyuan. In July 2026 the Ministry of Economic Affairs conditionally relaxed that for AI data centers within about 2 kilometers of the Datan or Hsieh-ho power plants, United Daily News reported. Taipower chairman Tseng Wen-sheng has compared an AI data center to a shot put: a container-sized unit using about as much power as a hotel, which could quickly overload a city grid.

No data center is under construction in Sharjah yet; what exists are agreements. The main plan is a Tier III data center from Khazna Sharjah, a joint venture of Khazna Data Centers and the Sharjah environmental company BEEAH, in the ComTec free zone in Kalba on the emirate's east coast. When the companies formed the venture in September 2022, they said their first Sharjah data center would have 9 megawatts of power capacity. No construction start or opening date has been announced.

In November 2024 the Sharjah Communication Technologies Authority (SCTA) signed a memorandum with the venture, promising regulatory oversight, land leases and power infrastructure, and called the Kalba site the emirate's largest data center to date. The partners said they were exploring power from BEEAH's Sharjah Waste to Energy plant and greywater recycling to cut water use. Khazna said in 2022 that the building would reuse and recycle wastewater and use solar power.

In January 2026 SCTA signed a second memorandum, with DataCanvas International and AI Caravan, to study building and running more data centers across Sharjah, including feasibility assessments for new sites, Economy Middle East reported. Khazna had first announced a Sharjah data center in 2019, with the digital company Evoteq, DCD reported.

Google's data center near Bridgeport is operating on the former Widows Creek coal plant site, and the company is investing another $1.5 billion in the campus through 2027. The two-building site opened in 2019 and leases land from the Tennessee Valley Authority. The current work expands that operating campus.

The site remains a major source of local tax revenue despite a 30-year state tax abatement. Jackson County Development Authority president Nathan Lee said Google contributed about $1.9 million to the county's tax base in 2025, much of it through the educational payment required by the abatement. Lee also said construction demand reopened Bridgeport's Tennessee River port to bring in sand after a decade without use, and filled local campgrounds and rental properties with workers.

Google says it will pay for the power and infrastructure needed for the expansion. It also pledged a $2 million fund with TVA and the Community Action Agency of Northeast Alabama for energy-efficiency work, primarily in Jackson County, plus $550,000 for school science kits. The $1.5 billion expansion is planned across 2026 and 2027.
unconfirmed: Rewritten by lane v from the hold list (5 searches). An Alabama Gazette opinion column (June 30, 2026) says Jackson County commissioners unanimously banned data centers effective June 23; the news reports behind that claim (WFSU, WUSF) are about Jackson County, Florida. The claim is wrong for this county and is not used.
The North Alabama Electric Cooperative item is the utility's own newsletter; it is used only for the date and venue of the announcement and Google's stated water position.
The 2011 Earthjustice and Sierra Club contamination finding is the groups' report as described by Data Center Knowledge before construction.
The expanded campus's water use, the dollar value of Google's abatement, and whether any public hearing was held were not found.

paragraphs: Crittenden County's data center is Google's $4 billion campus on about 1,100 acres of former farmland south of West Memphis, near the Mississippi River. Google broke ground in October 2025; West Memphis's development director said Elon Musk had looked at the site first, the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette reported. A Google subsidiary, Groot LLC, paid $16.5 million for 1,117 acres in November 2024. The city council approved up to $60 billion in industrial development bonds over 30 years, $10 billion for real estate and $50 billion for equipment. "Current development plans are confirmed for two buildings with the potential to expand," said Google's Laurel Brown. Mayor Marco McClendon called the announcement "the biggest day" in "Best Memphis" history, and contrasted it with xAI's gas turbines across the river: "We also accomplished this goal of this project without using any gas turbines," the Arkansas Advocate reported. Google applied for a Clean Air Act permit for backup generators. It set up a $25 million Energy Impact Fund for local bills and weatherization, in a city where 39 percent of school-age children lived in poverty at the 2020 census.

Power has become the fight. Entergy Arkansas, not the city utility, supplies the campus, partly through Cypress Solar, a 600-megawatt solar project. Entergy asked regulators for a $2.02 monthly rate increase on customers for the project, the Arkansas Times reported. Leaked details of Entergy's contract with Google appeared to show Google paying only part of Cypress Solar's cost, and Entergy filed a legal complaint against the Democrat-Gazette and the Arkansas Times over the leak. At a September 2026 legislative energy committee hearing, Entergy said Google would pay more than the full cost over a 20-year contract. "In my mind, I want to see that proved up," said Sen. Jimmy Hickey Jr. Water is less clear than first advertised. At the 2025 launch the Arkansas Times reported Google would cool with recycled wastewater, but in September 2026 Bob Atkins of West Memphis Utilities told legislators the first three of five buildings would use air conditioning, and he would not give a total water figure.
/data-centers/united-states/arkansas/cri.unconfirmed: KARK's story returned a 35-character shell. The Arkansas Times' September piece says the leaked documents appear to show Google paying only part of Cypress Solar; the Democrat-Gazette's own follow-up was not read. Google's jobs and investment figures are the company's. The '$1.1 billion in benefits' for Entergy customers is Entergy's claim and not stated. Action News 5's '300 jobs' is not repeated because Google itself said only 'hundreds'.

paragraphs: Pulaski County has two large data center projects and a year of fighting over them. At the Port of Little Rock, Google is behind "Project Boar", developed through a front company, Willowbend Capital, that bought 380 acres from the city. The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette identified Google in January 2026. A Clean Water Act permit application to the Army Corps of Engineers showed five industrial buildings totaling 1.43 million square feet, two office buildings and a substation, with about 16.8 acres of wetlands to be filled; it did not state water or power demand. The city's agreement gives Google at least a 65 percent property tax abatement for 30 years in return for annual payments starting at $300,000. City officials said they had signed nondisclosure agreements. "A final decision to build is only made after all diligence and public reviews are complete, and, candidly, we have not reached that point," Google's Laurel Brown said in June. Near Wrightsville, Connecticut-based AVAIO Digital plans a 760-acre campus with $6 billion of initial investment and 150MW of contracted power from Entergy Arkansas that could grow to 1 gigawatt, the Arkansas Times reported. Its project manager said water use would average about 200,000 gallons a day in warmer months.

On May 26 the Quorum Court appeared to pass a one-year moratorium on new data centers in unincorporated areas, with an eight-vote exemption for AVAIO, the Arkansas Advocate reported. "Arkansas is the Natural State, and tonight I heard, 'Natural State be damned. Money, money, money,'" resident Teri Drennan said. Two days later the county clerk announced she had miscounted: the emergency ordinance needed ten votes and had not passed. County Attorney Hamilton Kemp had questioned whether a 2023 state law allowed a ban at all. On July 28 the court voted down a new moratorium that also exempted AVAIO, after rejecting an amendment that would have made exempt projects follow future rules, KATV reported. Little Rock's Board of Directors unanimously adopted data center zoning rules on June 2 after a nearly five-hour meeting in which many residents asked for a moratorium instead. Mayor Frank Scott Jr. said the city could not ban data centers outright under Act 851 of 2023. Sierra Club chapter president George Wise said of Entergy's pledge that rates would not rise: "What's a pledge? What's a pledge? I don't believe it."
/data-centers/united-states/arkansas/pul.unconfirmed: The Quorum Court vote counts differ: at the meeting the clerk counted 10 in favour; Little Rock Public Radio counted 8 for, 5 against and 2 present. Whether Little Rock later adopted its proposed moratorium until January 2027 (reported as under consideration in July) was not confirmed. The Army Corps' count of over 1,100 public comments appeared only in a search summary. AVAIO's investment and power figures are the company's.

paragraphs: Carver County's data centers are in Chaska, where the city's own municipal electric utility is a draw for operators. The city already has a UnitedHealth Group data center and two Stream buildings; the new proposal is CloudHQ's roughly $1 billion, 1.4-million-square-foot campus on about 70 acres, with up to 180 megawatts of power and 75 to 100 jobs. Chaska's City Council gave it preliminary approval 4-1 on October 21, 2024, over objections from the neighboring Clover Ridge neighborhood.

"This is the largest economic development project we will ever see," Mayor Mark Windschitl said, while resident Susan Nelson said it "will impact my quality of life" and "decrease our property values." The city expects the project to use up to 1.5 million gallons of groundwater a day at peak; CloudHQ says it will use air-based chillers and signed no nondisclosure agreements. A new substation would connect directly to Xcel Energy's transmission line, pending a system impact study.

CloudHQ had not applied for final city approval as of the most recent public update. Elsewhere in the county, the city of Carver adopted its own one-year moratorium on new data centers on April 11, 2026, running through April 2027.

Elko New Market, in southern Scott County, has barred new data centers until May 13, 2027, or until it adopts permanent rules, whichever comes first. The City Council adopted the interim ordinance on May 14, 2026. While it is in force, the city will not accept or consider any planning or zoning application for a data center, and city staff are studying whether its zoning rules need to change.

The ordinance cites possible impacts on neighboring properties, "including but not limited to electricity and water consumption, and light and noise impacts." Water is a sore point in the city: when Elko New Market tested a higher pumping rate ahead of a planned water bottling plant, residents found "dark and murky water running through their pipes," the Star Tribune reported, caused by released manganese. Scott County's one operating data center is small, Compass Datacenters' 4.8-megawatt building in Shakopee.

Compass Datacenters is building an eight-building data center campus in the I-20/59 industrial park in Meridian, announced in January 2025 as a $10 billion investment, a figure that includes the computer equipment its customers will install. Groundwork began in June 2025 and the first building went under construction in February 2026. Each building is to be about 250,000 square feet with 40 megawatts of computing power, 320 megawatts in all, and Mississippi Power is to supply around 500 megawatts.

The pace depends on power. Compass expects to build roughly one building a year for eight years, the Meridian Star reported, while Bill Hannah of the East Mississippi Business Development Corporation said the goal is "to have two buildings complete and operational by December of '26." The state gave Compass 10-year income and franchise tax exemptions. Compass says each building will employ about 30 people, 240 to 300 in all, and use a closed-loop cooling system that will not draw continuously on local water.

At a Board of Supervisors meeting on May 18, 2026, residents questioned the project's transparency, noise, generator emissions, property values and air quality. Megan Clearman said the public had not been given enough information about the project or its impacts. Supervisors answered that such projects often begin under confidentiality agreements and that the tax revenue could pay for roads, bridges and schools. "I would rather be on the front end of something than to be on the rear end of anything," Supervisor Joe Norwood told officials from other counties in September.

No large data center has been proposed in Hillsborough County. Its data centers are small ones that rent server space to businesses. The best known is FirstLight's at 8 Commerce Drive in Bedford, 7,250 square feet inside a three-story office building, which ColoSpace opened around 2006 and FirstLight bought in 2019. In March 2026 FirstLight added about 25 percent more space there, with power and cooling for up to 100 more racks of servers.

Power is the barrier to anything bigger. Eversource, the state's largest utility, received data center requests adding up to 1,500 megawatts of power in the fall of 2025, while New Hampshire's own plants produce about 4,500 megawatts, roughly half of what the state uses. Eversource engineering chief Digaunto Chatterjee said a very large data center would need to sit near generators and high-voltage lines, most of them in the Manchester-Nashua-Portsmouth triangle. "You have a system that is stable. Don't mess it up is what I'm getting at," he told NH Business Review.

Two local legislators split on a 2026 bill, House Bill 1265, to pause large data center construction while the state studies it. "We have a drought in New Hampshire and we need to put up guardrails in front of the train," said Rep. Wendy Thomas, D-Merrimack. Rep. Carry Spier, D-Nashua, noted that small data centers in Bedford, Manchester and Salem do not cause the problems the bill's sponsor described. Gov. Kelly Ayotte has said she will propose a statewide data center moratorium in her next budget.

No data center has been proposed inside Cayuga County, but a project just across its border in the town of Lansing, Tompkins County, has pushed several county towns to pass their own moratoriums. TeraWulf wants to build an AI data center at the former Cayuga coal plant on Cayuga Lake's east shore, starting at 50 megawatts of power in 2026 and growing to as much as 400 megawatts by 2029. It has promised about 100 jobs and closed-loop cooling that uses only a few gallons of water a day, though its 2025 press release had listed an "industrial-scale water intake system" among the site's assets.

Towns responded fast. The Town of Victory adopted an 18-month moratorium; Mentz and Scipio have sent one-year moratoriums to the county's law committee for review, wider than the state's pause because they would cover data centers of any size. Mentz Supervisor Mark Emerson pointed to the Seneca River, which flows into Cayuga Lake through his town: "So we don't want the pollution on our northern border," he said, adding "our electricity bills would be out of this world." Scipio Supervisor Gary Mutchler wrote that the moratorium protects "our beautiful Finger Lakes region without major commercial industry."

The City of Auburn went further. On July 9, 2026, its council voted unanimously to urge Governor Kathy Hochul to sign the statewide one-year data center moratorium the Legislature had passed, and on August 6 it adopted its own 12-month local moratorium, 5-0, while it rewrites its land-use rules. Planning director Stephen Selvek said the local rule fills a gap because the state's plan targets only facilities of 50 megawatts or more. Councilor Christina Calarco pointed to Owasco Lake, the city's drinking water source: "Our lakes are our most valuable asset," she said. Mentz and Scipio's boards are expected to act on their own moratoriums once the county's law committee finishes its review.

Google is building a data center campus on about 400 acres of state-owned land in Stillwater, the Payne County seat, bordered by East Richmond Road, East Airport Road, North Perkins Road and North Jardot Road. Through most of the approval process the project went by the name of a subsidiary, Kipper LLC, before Google was confirmed as the company behind it. The plan allows up to six buildings worth $500 million each, for a potential $3 billion total, with the first phase possible as early as 2027.

The city council approved an economic development deal in which Kipper makes annual payments to local taxing entities instead of property taxes, an initial $867,568 for Phase 1, tied to a minimum $500 million investment and at least 30 jobs per phase. Mayor Will Joyce called it the biggest economic development action the city has ever taken. Because Stillwater's electric utility is public, state law required a public vote before OG&E could serve the campus: residents approved the franchise 10,250 to 3,930, which will pay the city about $2.25 million per data center a year once running.

OG&E has agreed to power this site and two Google campuses in Muskogee, with the combined load reaching 1 gigawatt within five years and peaking at 1.2 gigawatts by 2036; Google is paying to connect all three to the grid and is building two solar farms on OG&E's system. In September 2026 the Oklahoma Corporation Commission, the state's utility regulator, opened its review of those contracts; a commission official testified the deals "feature reasonable protections for ratepayers."

Water has divided local officials. Payne County Commissioner Rhonda Markum said nearby residents worry about the drought and the project's power and water use, and that flooding hit the construction site on April 30. She said county commissioners are bound by a non-disclosure agreement and have had no direct contact with Google. Stillwater City Manager Brady Moore said the city's first two phases are allotted 2.7 million gallons of water a day out of 3.2 million gallons set aside for growth in that part of the city, and any further building would require Google to invest in the water treatment plant.

Andrews County's one tracked project is Stingray, a 100-megawatt computing campus that Cipher Digital, formerly Cipher Mining, is building on a 250-acre site west of the city of Andrews for Amazon, which will lease it for 15 years. Cipher closed on the site in late 2024 and in June 2026 raised $810 million in high-yield bonds to pay the remaining construction costs, Bloomberg and The Next Web reported. At a town hall on July 14, 2026, officials said work had only reached the stage of clearing dirt, and it was still unclear when construction would begin.

At that town hall, Cipher representatives unveiled a water plan: the campus would use reverse osmosis to treat brackish water from a deep aquifer that isn't fit for cattle or irrigation, said chief construction officer Christopher Totin. Residents shouted that the facility has "no right in Andrews County" and said they were being treated as guinea pigs. "What assurances do we have from you that this is not just empty promises?" one resident asked; another said of runoff, "The cattle will eat it, the grass will take it, and we'll take the loss."

Cipher's representatives said the campus would be the first to go offline in a countywide energy crisis, estimated its sound at about 38 decibels, and cited at least 50 full-time jobs and $162 million in tax revenue over 20 years. Amazon is reportedly the tenant, but the company would not confirm it because the tenant had asked to stay anonymous.

Fort Bend County's only recorded project is Lambda Houston, a data center ECL is proposing at the former ECL TerraSite in Sugar Land; its status beyond "proposed" and its power use have not surfaced. The county's clearer story so far is regulation written before any project arrived: Missouri City, a city of more than 78,000 with no data center inside its limits, passed new zoning rules in May 2026 requiring any proposed data center to disclose its expected energy and water use before getting a building permit, and to hold public hearings before a special use permit is granted, Houston Public Media reported.

City staff called it preparation, not a ban. "This gives us the proactive ability to create the standards that we want to see for locations within the city of where they would be appropriate," said Development Services Director Jennifer Thomas Gomez. The industry pushed back: Data Center Coalition vice president Dan Diorio said water-use worries are "a common misconception." Donna Thomas of the Fort Bend County Environmental Organization disagreed: "People don't realize what that's going to do to your water ... it's going to impact the water that we have."

Missouri City's move is part of a wider pattern. In September 2026 The Real Deal counted dozens of Texas cities and counties with data center moratoriums, bans or special-permit rules, and listed Missouri City as Fort Bend County's entry. The magazine noted Gov. Greg Abbott had ordered a statewide pause on new data centers connecting to the grid until regulators audit their power and water use.
